Sensation ends once receptors encode the physical stimulation; perception is the brain's interpretation of that code
Sensation and perception are a single continuous process with no meaningful dividing line
Sensation covers touch and taste, while perception covers vision and hearing
explain: The peripheral receptors' job stops at producing a neural code of local pressure and temperature. Everything after that — combining millions of measurements and matching them against stored knowledge of objects — is perception, carried out by the brain.
hint: Draw the line where measurement hands off to interpretation, not where the object gets named.

q: Most sensory receptors fire more vigorously as stimulation grows stronger. One receptor family works in reverse: stronger stimulation lowers its release of neurotransmitter. Which is it?
options: Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
Chemoreceptors
Photoreceptors
explain: Photoreceptors are the odd family out: increased light energy reduces the neurotransmitter they release, the opposite of pressure-, heat-, and chemical-sensitive receptors, which answer stronger stimulation with more vigorous activity.
hint: Think of the receptor family whose stimulus arrives at the speed of light.

q: Mid-somersault off the high dive, a diver knows with her eyes shut exactly where her arms are and whether she is tilting off axis. Which senses is she relying on?
options: Exteroception, because her limbs lie outside the central nervous system
Proprioception for limb position plus equilibrioception for balance
Touch receptors in the skin registering changes in air pressure as she rotates through the air
Nociception, the sense of bodily damage, repurposed to signal orientation
explain: Both are forms of interoception, senses aimed at the body itself: proprioception reports where the limbs sit in space, and equilibrioception reports balance. Neither depends on the eyes or on any signal from the outside environment.
hint: She is sensing her own body rather than the environment — two inward-facing senses are involved.

q: The retina delivers what amounts to a huge two-dimensional grid of light-intensity measurements, yet what you experience is a stable three-dimensional world of recognizable objects. What does this gap force us to conclude?
options: Perception must be an active inference, because the sensory data alone underdetermine what is out there
The retina itself must contain a complete three-dimensional model that the brain simply reads out
Experience is an unprocessed copy of the retinal image, so the gap is only apparent
Depth and identity must reach the brain through separate nonvisual channels such as the vestibular organs and neck muscles
explain: Countless different worlds could have produced the same grid of measurements, so the brain must go beyond the data — combining cues, prior experience, and built-in assumptions to construct its best guess about what is actually out there.
hint: Ask whether the numbers arriving from the eye are enough, on their own, to specify one unique world.

q: On a moonless camping trip the forest is visible only in shades of gray, and the fine print on a map is impossible to read. Which photoreceptors are carrying the load, and why is the scene colorless?
options: Cones, which trade away all color vision in exchange for extreme light sensitivity after the sun goes down
Rods, which need very little light but come in a single variety and so cannot signal color
Rods, which switch among three pigments too slowly to keep up in darkness
Cones in the fovea, which suspend color processing to conserve energy at night
explain: Rods are far more light-sensitive than cones, so they dominate in dim conditions — but every rod responds the same way across wavelengths, making night vision colorless, and their lower resolution blurs fine detail like small print.
hint: One receptor type thrives in dim light but responds identically to every wavelength.

q: As a friend walks away down a long hallway, the image she casts on your retina shrinks steadily — and the light from her head lands on the lower part of it. What explains both facts?
options: The lens actively rescales and flips each image to protect the fovea from overload
Retinal neurons migrate across the eye to track objects as they move through the scene
Light must pass through the small opening of the pupil, producing an inverted, perspective-projected image
The brain deliberately shrinks the appearance of distant objects after the fact so the visual field stays uncluttered
explain: Because all light funnels through the small pupil, geometry takes over: rays cross, so light from above lands low on the retina, and more distant objects project smaller images — a size change the brain can later exploit as a depth cue.
hint: Think about what a small aperture does to the geometry of incoming light rays.

q: One cortical neuron fires only for short edges tilted about 45 degrees; another, much farther along the visual pathway, fires selectively for faces. What organizing principle does this contrast illustrate?
options: Lateral inhibition: neurons suppress their neighbors to sharpen contrast at boundaries
Hierarchical processing: preferred features grow more complex and specific at each successive stage
Functional equivalence: every visual neuron responds to every stimulus, differing only in firing rate
Parallel segregation: edge and face information travel entirely separate routes beginning at the retina itself
explain: The visual system is built as a hierarchy: Hubel and Wiesel (1959) found early cortical cells with receptive fields tuned to simple oriented edges, while regions farther along respond to complex shapes and finally to specific categories such as faces or places.
hint: Compare what neurons prefer early in the pathway with what they prefer many stages later.

q: Along the coiled basilar membrane of the cochlea, hair cells near the entrance respond to high frequencies while cells deeper into the coil respond to progressively lower ones. What is this systematic layout called?
options: A tonotopic map
A cortical homunculus
A phonemic hierarchy
An equal-loudness contour
explain: The cochlea sorts sound by frequency along its coil — a tonotopic map that is preserved as the signal travels through subcortical structures up to the auditory cortex. The homunculus, by contrast, is the body map found in somatosensory cortex.
hint: Frequencies are arranged in an orderly spatial sequence, like keys laid out along a piano.

q: Gauthier and Tarr (1997) trained volunteers for days to discriminate Greebles, novel computer-generated creatures. Afterward, viewing Greebles activated the fusiform face area, a region long tied to faces. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Greebles get processed as literal faces because their parts sit in a roughly face-like arrangement
That region supports expert fine discrimination among similar items, not faces specifically
Face processing relocated to another area, freeing the fusiform region to handle Greebles
The activity reflected motor planning for naming the creatures rather than visual analysis
explain: Because brand-new expertise with non-face objects recruited the same region, Gauthier and Tarr argued the fusiform area is tuned to expert discrimination of visually similar items — faces engage it because nearly everyone becomes a face expert through social life.
hint: Ask what faces and well-practiced Greeble judgments share as a processing demand.

q: Patient DF, who had ventral-stream damage, could not report a slot's orientation aloud, yet she smoothly rotated a card to post it through that very slot. What should a patient with the reverse lesion — dorsal damage, ventral intact — show?
options: Accurate verbal reports of orientation but clumsy, poorly guided reaching and posting
Failure on both tasks, since the two streams cannot operate independently of each other
Normal performance on both tasks after sufficient practice with feedback
Accurate posting but chance-level verbal reports, exactly like DF herself
explain: Goodale and Milner (1991) described exactly this double dissociation: dorsal damage spares conscious perceptual judgment but wrecks visually guided action — the mirror image of DF. They reframed the two streams as perception versus action rather than what versus where.
hint: A double dissociation predicts the mirror-image pattern of spared and broken abilities.

q: Reading a friend's terrible handwriting, you decipher a mangled scribble instantly because the sentence so far makes only one word plausible. Which kind of processing filled the gap?
options: Bottom-up processing, driven entirely by the physical pattern of ink marks on the page
Transduction, converting the ink pattern into a neural code
Direct perception, guiding the eyes without any internal interpretation
Top-down processing, applying stored knowledge and expectation to the input
explain: When context and prior knowledge shape how raw input is read, that is top-down processing. Bottom-up processing works purely from the stimulus itself, which in this case was too degraded to settle the word on its own.
hint: The decisive information came from what you already knew, not from the marks themselves.

q: Helmholtz (1867) famously described perception as 'unconscious inference.' Which claim best captures the idea?
options: The brain automatically constructs its best guess about the world from ambiguous sensory evidence, outside awareness
Perception begins as deliberate conscious reasoning in infancy and only gradually becomes automatic through years of repetition
Each sensory nerve routes its stimulus directly to a fixed behavior with no interpretation in between
We perceive only the input we consciously attend to and suppress the rest
explain: Helmholtz argued perception works like reasoning without awareness: the brain treats sensory data as evidence and settles on the most probable external cause. This launched the constructive tradition, breaking from his teacher Muller's direct nerve-to-behavior pathways.
hint: Both words in the famous phrase matter: the process resembles reasoning, yet you never feel yourself doing it.

q: Crossing a room toward a doorway, you might simply keep the doorway centered in your visual field and correct continuously as you move — no internal 3D map required. Whose theory does this describe, and what is its key claim?
options: Helmholtz's constructive account: the brain first infers a full mental model of the room and then steers the body through it
The Gestalt account: the doorway is grouped from its parts by proximity and similarity
Gibson's direct perception: stimulus properties guide action in a continuous perception-action loop
The template account: the doorway is matched point by point against a stored doorway image
explain: Gibson rejected intermediate mental models, proposing that perception serves action directly: properties of the changing stimulus, like where the doorway sits in the visual field, continuously steer behavior in a perception-action loop.
hint: One theorist insisted no intermediate mental model is needed between stimulus and movement.

q: A marching band scatters across a field, yet the drummers in red instantly read as one group and the trumpeters in blue as another, regardless of who stands near whom. Which Gestalt principle is doing the work?
options: Good continuation
Proximity
Closure
Similarity
explain: The law of similarity groups elements that share a property such as color or shape, and here it overrides spacing entirely. Proximity would instead group whoever happens to stand closest together, which is not what you experience in this scene.
hint: Notice which cue wins when spacing and shared appearance point to different groupings.

q: Your eyes jump several times each second, and every jump replaces the entire retinal image, yet the world appears rock-steady. Why is this taken as evidence for constructive rather than direct accounts of perception?
options: It shows the eye muscles physically stabilize the image before it ever reaches the brain
It shows perception happens too quickly for any interpretive processing to intervene
It shows experience tracks a stable internal model even while the raw input churns
It shows that motion detection is completed entirely within the retina itself
explain: Steadiness despite constantly replaced input implies the brain maintains something beyond the input: an inferred model of the scene that persists across eye movements. Accounts that tie experience tightly to the momentary stimulus struggle to explain this stability.
hint: Compare how much the input changes with how little the experience does, then ask what must be added.

q: In a recording, a cough fully replaces one speech sound in a sentence, yet listeners insist they heard the complete word and often cannot even say where the cough occurred. What does this phonemic restoration effect reveal?
options: The auditory system amplifies faint sounds that survive underneath louder masking noise
Listeners quietly rebuild the sentence from long-term memory well after hearing it, rather than during perception
The ear's own mechanical filtering strips the cough away before transduction happens
Language knowledge supplies the missing sound, merging top-down expectation with bottom-up input
explain: The replaced sound was never in the signal, so hearing it must come from knowledge of how the language sounds — a top-down contribution fused seamlessly with bottom-up analysis of the sounds genuinely present. The filling-in happens during perception, not in later recall.
hint: The restored sound physically is not in the recording — ask where else it could come from.

q: From a train window, fence posts beside the track whip past in a blur while distant hills barely crawl. Which depth cue is at work?
options: Binocular disparity
Occlusion
Motion parallax
The convexity bias
explain: Motion parallax is the depth cue based on movement: as the observer travels, nearby objects shift across the retina much faster than far ones, so relative image speed reveals relative distance — no second eye required.
hint: This cue needs movement by the observer and works fine with one eye closed.

q: Hold a finger near your nose, stare at a distant clock, and close each eye in turn: the finger leaps left and right while the clock barely shifts. What is the visual system extracting from this difference between the two eyes?
options: Relative depth, computed from binocular disparity — the basis of stereopsis
Object identity, computed from whichever retina receives the sharper image
Surface reflectance, computed from the luminance ratio between the two views
Motion parallax, computed from the small head movements made as each eye opens and closes
explain: Each eye views the scene from a slightly different position, so features land at different retinal locations — binocular disparity. The size of that offset varies with distance from the fixation point, and the brain converts it into depth through stereopsis.
hint: Two vantage points a few centimeters apart disagree more about near things than far things.

q: In Adelson's checkerboard illusion, two squares send physically identical light to the eye, yet the one lying in apparent shadow looks much lighter. What is the visual system actually trying to compute?
options: The raw quantity of light arriving from each surface, measured as precisely as possible
The stable reflectance of each surface, with the current illumination discounted
The wavelength composition of the shadowed region compared with the lit region
The retinal size of each square relative to the object casting the shadow
explain: Raw light levels swing wildly with lighting — a black road in sunlight can send the eye far more light than white paper indoors — so the brain estimates reflectance, the stable surface property, by factoring in the apparent illumination. The illusion exposes that correction at work.
hint: Ask which property of a black backpack stays the same indoors and outdoors, and which changes constantly.

q: A borzoi — a breed you have never seen before — trots past, and you instantly think 'dog.' Why does this everyday feat embarrass template models of recognition?
options: Templates fail only for man-made objects, and a borzoi is a natural kind
The stored dog template simply updates too slowly to cover newly bred varieties
No stored image can match a never-seen exemplar point for point, so recognition must lean on shared features
Dogs are actually recognized by their gait and motion signatures alone, so no stored image comparison ever occurs
explain: Classification means recognizing a brand-new exemplar as a category member. A template scheme needs a stored image to align with the input, and none exists for a first encounter — whereas feature-based schemes can match the borzoi's dog-typical parts and proportions.
hint: A point-by-point match requires having stored something nearly identical beforehand.

q: Biederman (1972) showed objects are recognized faster and more accurately in scenes where they belong, and Barenholtz (2014) found people can identify far blurrier objects when photographed in their own homes. Which concept unites these findings?
options: Scene schemas: learned expectations about which objects appear where provide top-down support
Foveal magnification: familiar environments draw the retina's high-resolution center to the right spots more quickly
Motion parallax: well-known rooms supply richer depth information during scanning
Edge detection: household lighting happens to produce unusually strong luminance boundaries
explain: A scene schema is stored knowledge of which objects belong in which settings. It lets context stand in for missing image detail, which is why degraded objects are easiest to identify in a highly familiar place and hardest with no context at all.
hint: Both results show recognition borrowing information from the surroundings rather than the object itself.

q: A rotating mask viewed from its hollow back should look concave — the nose tip really is the farthest point — yet observers stubbornly see a normal face bulging outward. Which account best explains the error?
options: The mask's paint and shadows make its sensory input genuinely identical to a convex face's input
A lifetime prior that faces bulge outward overrides the bottom-up depth cues
The visual system is simply incapable of representing concave surfaces of any kind
Attention locks onto the eyes and mouth, which prevents any depth analysis from finishing
explain: The hollow face illusion is a top-down depth effect: virtually every face ever encountered is convex, so the brain bets on convexity even when bottom-up cues argue otherwise. Illusions like this expose the assumptions perception normally runs on unnoticed.
hint: Consider what shape essentially every face you have ever encountered has had.

q: Stare at a wireframe cube drawing long enough and its front face abruptly becomes its back face, then flips again — the ink never changes, only your experience. What does such bi-stability demonstrate?
options: The retina fatigues and briefly transmits a mirror-reversed image during each flip
Tiny eye movements physically rotate the cube's projection on the retina
The two eyes take turns dominating awareness, alternating between the left-eye image and the right-eye image
One stimulus can support two interpretations, so the percept is the brain's revisable guess
explain: A flat drawing is consistent with two different three-dimensional cubes, and with no evidence to break the tie the brain alternates between them. The Necker cube thus shows perception is an interpretation of ambiguous data, not a direct readout of the stimulus.
hint: Nothing on the page changes during a flip — so locate the change somewhere else.

q: A 3x3 kernel holding a diagonal pattern of ones is multiplied cell by cell against a 3x3 patch of an image, and the products are summed. The result comes out high. What does that high number indicate?
options: The patch closely matches the feature the kernel is tuned to detect
The patch contains more active pixels than the kernel can represent
The image has been compressed with almost no loss of information
The network has finished training and its weights are now frozen
explain: A convolution acts as a match detector: when bright pixels line up with the kernel's high weights, the products sum to a large value, and when they misalign the sum stays small. Each kernel therefore scores how strongly its particular feature is present.
hint: Think about when multiplying two aligned grids and summing would produce the biggest total.

q: Rather than being applied to one spot, a convolutional kernel is slid across the whole image, yielding a map of responses at every location. What problem does the sliding solve?
options: It prevents the network's output from ever collapsing to zero during the training process
It lets a single learned feature be detected wherever in the image it happens to appear
It guarantees color images are processed as faithfully as grayscale ones
It reduces the number of pixels the camera sensor needs to capture in the first place
explain: Sliding one kernel across all positions produces a feature map: the same detector fires whether its pattern shows up in a corner or dead center. That gives the network tolerance to location, a basic requirement for recognizing objects in real photographs.
hint: A cat can appear in any corner of a photograph — the detector has to travel.

q: For decades, computer vision ran on features hand-designed by engineers and succeeded mainly in controlled settings like assembly lines and mail sorting. What key change let CNNs crack everyday object recognition?
options: Computers began storing an exhaustive template photograph of every object from every possible viewpoint
Engineers finally discovered the single correct feature set through systematic trial and error
The networks learn their own features from data, tuning connection weights to optimize task performance
Camera hardware improved enough that raw images no longer required any processing at all
explain: Hand-crafting features that survive real-world variation proved nearly impossible — a struggle dating back to MIT's optimistic Summer Vision Project of 1966. CNNs sidestep it by learning which features matter directly from labeled examples during training.
hint: The breakthrough was about who, or what, decides which features are worth detecting.

q: Train a CNN to categorize photographs and its early layers develop oriented-edge detectors while later layers respond to whole objects. Why does this pattern excite vision researchers?
options: It proves that sufficiently deep artificial networks are conscious in essentially the same way biological brains are
It shows such networks can reach high accuracy without any training data
It means experiments on biological vision are no longer needed at all
The learned progression mirrors the cortical hierarchy, from edge-tuned cells to object-selective regions
explain: Nobody told the network to build edge detectors — they emerged from learning, echoing the biological pathway Hubel and Wiesel (1959) began charting, which runs from simple oriented-edge cells toward object-selective cortex. The convergence hints at shared computational principles.
hint: Compare the network's layer-by-layer features with what recording electrodes find along the visual pathway.

q: When an artificial network must represent images using only a handful of active hidden units at a time, the features it learns come to resemble the edge-tuned receptive fields Hubel and Wiesel recorded in cat cortex. What does this convergence suggest?
options: Edge detectors can emerge only in biological tissue, so the resemblance is a coincidence
Every network, however it is constrained, learns an identical feature set in the end
The brain may likewise rely on a sparse code, with few neurons active per stimulus
Such networks are simply memorizing the training images rather than learning features
explain: The telling detail is the constraint: cortex-like features appear specifically when the network is forced toward sparseness. If the same coding pressure yields the same features, the brain's edge detectors may reflect its own use of a sparse encoding scheme.
hint: Focus on the specific constraint that made the artificial features turn brain-like.

q: A person names a hopelessly blurred object at a glance because it sits on their own kitchen counter, while a feedforward CNN trained on isolated object photos fails on the very same image. Which difference best explains the gap?
options: The network lacks a fovea, so it cannot sample any region at high resolution
Human optics outresolve any camera sensor, so the person effectively received a much sharper image to work with
The network has too few layers to extract edges from blurred input of any kind
Humans recruit top-down scene knowledge, while a feedforward pass consumes only the pixels
explain: Barenholtz (2014) showed familiar context slashes the resolution people need for recognition — knowledge of what belongs on that counter does work the pixels cannot. A purely feedforward network is bottom-up only, with no scene expectations to draw on.
hint: One recognizer brings expectations about the setting; the other brings nothing but the image.

q: Your eyes alone send the brain tens of millions of light measurements many times per second, yet you experience one coherent scene. What does this gap between input and experience reveal about cognition?
options: Sensory receptors discard most information before it ever reaches the brain
Conscious experience is a complete, faithful copy of the sensory input, merely compressed for efficient storage
Processing capacity is limited, so a mechanism must select which inputs get deep analysis
The brain processes everything fully but forgets nearly all of it within seconds
explain: The brain cannot fully analyze everything the senses deliver, so attention acts as the selection process deciding which inputs receive deep processing. The bottleneck sits in central processing, not in the receptors, which transduce signals regardless of where attention is aimed.
hint: Ask whether the bottleneck lies in the sense organs themselves or somewhere further along the processing stream.

q: At a crowded reception you effortlessly follow your friend's voice while a dozen other conversations blur into murmur. Which phenomenon does this illustrate?
options: The cocktail party effect
Inattentional deafness
Auditory perceptual constancy
The ventriloquist effect
explain: Selectively tuning in to one voice among many competing streams is the cocktail party effect, the everyday phenomenon that dichotic listening research was designed to simulate. Inattentional deafness is the failure to hear sounds under heavy load, and the other terms concern stability and localization of sound, not voice selection.
hint: Focus on the act of selecting one auditory stream while all the others fade into background noise.

q: In Cherry's (1953) dichotic listening studies, participants repeated aloud the message played to one ear while a second message played to the other ear. What was the main purpose of the repeat-aloud requirement?
options: To measure how quickly and accurately participants could articulate rapid speech under time pressure
To guarantee attention stayed locked on one channel so the other stream was genuinely unattended
To train participants to divide attention equally between the two ears
To check whether hearing is more accurate in the right ear than in the left
explain: Shadowing forces continuous engagement with the designated channel: if the voice is being echoed accurately, the listener must be attending to it. That makes the opposite ear's stream truly unattended, letting researchers probe how much of an ignored message still gets processed.
hint: Consider what the researcher must be certain of before drawing any conclusions about the ignored ear.

q: Midway through a shadowing session, the ignored ear's message switches from English to German, and later the speaker changes from a man to a woman. What does dichotic listening research predict the listener will notice?
options: Both changes, since novelty always captures attention
The language switch but not the voice change
Neither change, because the ignored ear is completely blocked from processing
The voice change but not the language switch
explain: Cherry found listeners register coarse physical properties of an ignored stream, such as a shift in voice pitch or gender, while missing content-level changes like a switch of language. The filter passes surface features through but blocks meaning-level analysis of the unattended channel.
hint: Sort the two changes into physical characteristics versus content that requires comprehension to detect.

q: Moray (1959) played the same short word list dozens of times to the ignored ear during shadowing. Afterward, listeners failed to recognize any of those words. What is the strongest conclusion this result supports?
options: Without attention, the words' identities were never encoded, no matter how many times they repeated
Auditory memories decay completely within a few seconds regardless of attention
Participants fully encoded the words but then deliberately suppressed them from their reports as irrelevant
Errors in shadowing prevented listeners from hearing the ignored ear clearly
explain: Even massive repetition left no recognizable trace, suggesting unattended words were rejected before their identities were registered — consistent with content being filtered early. Rapid decay or deliberate suppression cannot explain why physical features of the same stream were still noticed.
hint: Ask what thirty separate presentations should have accomplished if the words were being identified at all.

q: A radiologist scans an X-ray while tuning out hallway chatter; later she eats lunch while answering email. Which pairing correctly labels the two situations?
options: First divided attention, then selective attention
Both are selective attention, since a target is chosen in each case
First selective attention, then divided attention
Both are divided attention, since multiple stimuli are present in each case
explain: Focusing on one stream while excluding competitors is selective attention; distributing resources across two concurrent tasks is divided attention. Merely having other stimuli nearby does not make attention divided — what matters is how many tasks are actively being pursued at once.
hint: Count how many tasks are actively being performed in each scene, not how many stimuli happen to exist.

q: In Broadbent's (1958) filter model, incoming streams are held briefly in a sensory store before one is passed along for deeper analysis. On what basis does the filter make its selection?
options: The emotional significance of each competing message
Physical characteristics such as voice pitch or spatial location
The semantic fit between each message and the listener's current goals
The grammatical complexity of each competing message
explain: Broadbent placed the filter before meaning is computed: selection runs on surface features like pitch, loudness, or location, and only the chosen stream reaches the detector that identifies words. Emotional or semantic screening would require exactly the meaning analysis the model says unattended input never receives.
hint: This is an early-selection model — work out what information is even available at that early stage.

q: During a shadowing session, a listener suddenly perks up because her name was spoken in the ear she was ignoring. Why is this a problem for a strict early-selection account?
options: It shows the sensory store retains unattended information far longer than the model's brief buffer allows
It shows listeners were secretly switching ears throughout the session
It shows physical features of ignored input are never analyzed at all
Recognizing a name requires identifying its meaning, which the filter supposedly blocked
explain: A name can only break through if the ignored stream was analyzed deeply enough to identify the word — precisely the processing an early filter is supposed to prevent. Moray's (1959) demonstration of this effect pushed theorists toward attenuation and late-selection alternatives.
hint: Work out what level of processing must occur before a sound can be recognized as your own name.

q: Gray and Wedderburn (1960) alternated a meaningful phrase between the ears — 'Dear' left, 'Aunt' right, 'Jane' left — while numbers filled the gaps in the opposite ear. Told to follow one ear only, what did participants typically report?
options: The meaningful phrase, stitched together across both ears
Only the items from the designated ear, an odd mix of words and numbers
Only the numbers, because digits are easier to retain than words
Nothing coherent, because switching between ears abolished comprehension
explain: Listeners chased the message's meaning as it hopped between ears, reporting the intact phrase rather than the ear-faithful jumble of words and digits. Tracking semantic continuity across channels means the supposedly unattended ear was being understood, which a purely physical filter cannot accommodate.
hint: Notice what would have to be processed for someone to follow a message as it jumps from ear to ear.

q: Treisman's (1964) attenuation account keeps selection early but changes what the filter does. In her model, what happens to an unattended stream?
options: It is stored intact and reviewed only if the attended stream pauses
It is blocked completely unless the listener deliberately switches channels
It is weakened like a turned-down volume, yet important or expected words can still be recognized
It is fully analyzed for meaning in parallel with the attended stream, and selection happens only just before the response stage
explain: Attenuation treats the filter as a dimmer rather than an on-off switch: the ignored signal survives in degraded form, and items with permanently low thresholds — your own name, contextually predicted words — can still reach recognition. Complete blocking is Broadbent's position; full parallel semantic analysis is late selection.
hint: Her model sits between complete blocking and complete analysis — look for the middle path.

q: Listeners shadowed the sentence 'The boys threw rocks at the bank' while the word 'money' repeated in the ignored ear (Mackay, 1973). Later they interpreted the sentence as being about a financial bank — yet denied ever hearing 'money.' What does this pattern show?
options: Ignored input is stored in conscious memory at first but is completely forgotten within about a minute of presentation
Ignored input can be processed for meaning and bias interpretation without ever reaching awareness
Ambiguous words are always resolved toward their most frequent everyday sense
Shadowing is too demanding for listeners to comprehend the attended sentence
explain: The ignored word steered which sense of 'bank' listeners settled on even though it never became conscious, so semantic processing occurred outside awareness. A filter that discarded unattended input before meaning could not produce this bias, showing that filtering is far more flexible than strict early models claim.
hint: Separate two questions — was the word consciously heard, and did its meaning nonetheless have an effect?

q: In Lavie's (1995) search task, an irrelevant peripheral letter slowed responses when the central search was easy but had no effect when the search was hard. How does load theory explain this?
options: Hard searches motivate participants, so they try harder to ignore everything
Easy searches encourage participants to move their eyes toward the periphery, which is exactly where the distractor sits
Hard searches cause fatigue, which happens to suppress distractor processing too
Easy tasks leave spare capacity that spills over onto the distractor; demanding tasks consume it all
explain: Perceptual capacity is spent involuntarily: whatever the central task does not use flows to irrelevant items, so distractors get processed under low load whether we want them to or not. High-load tasks exhaust capacity, leaving nothing for the flanker — selection by exhaustion rather than by a fixed gate.
hint: Think of attention as a fixed budget and ask where any unspent portion of it ends up going.

q: Green and Bavelier (2003) found action gamers were slowed by an irrelevant flanker even in the demanding version of a load task, where non-gamers showed no flanker effect — and novices trained on an action game later showed the same pattern. What is the best interpretation?
options: Gaming enlarges attentional capacity, so spare resources remain even under heavy demands
Gamers habitually ignore instructions and search displays in a fast but disorganized, scattershot fashion
Gamers respond so quickly that flanker effects become easier to measure statistically
People born with unusual attention profiles are simply drawn to gaming in the first place
explain: Within load theory, distractor processing signals leftover capacity, so showing it under high load implies gamers have more total resources to spend. The training study rules out pure self-selection: novices developed the same signature after practice, meaning the experience itself changed attentional capacity.
hint: Under load theory, distraction during a demanding task is a clue about total resources — and the trained-novice group settles the causal question.

q: People who traded instant messages while working through a reading passage took much longer to get through it (Fox, Rosen, & Crawford, 2009). Which principle best captures why?
options: Reading comprehension is impossible without complete silence
Text on screens is inherently harder to process than text on paper
Two concurrent tasks draw on the same limited pool of resources, so each gets less
Messaging engages the brain's language areas, and two language-based tasks never interfere with one another
explain: Splitting attention across simultaneous tasks means neither receives full resources, and performance costs follow — slower reading and weaker comprehension. The interference reflects a shared central bottleneck rather than anything special about screens or the need for silence.
hint: Ask what both messaging and reading are drawing from at the very same moment.

q: A legislator proposes banning handheld phones while driving but permitting hands-free calls, reasoning that freeing the hands removes the danger. What does dual-task driving research (Strayer & Johnston, 2001) say about this reasoning?
options: It is sound — steering with both hands eliminates most of the impairment
It is partly sound — hands-free calling impairs only inexperienced drivers who have not yet automatized vehicle control
It is backwards — holding the phone is protective because it keeps drivers alert
It misses the point — the impairment comes from the conversation's demands on processing, not from occupied hands
explain: Drivers on the phone missed stop signals far more often and braked more slowly, and handheld versus hands-free made no significant difference. The conversation itself competes with driving for central resources, so a law targeting only the hands leaves the real source of interference untouched.
hint: Locate the bottleneck precisely — is it in the hands, or in central processing resources?

q: Simulator studies compared drivers conversing with a passenger in the car against drivers conversing on a cell phone (Drews et al., 2008). What did they find?
options: Both conversation types impaired driving equally, since talking is talking
Phone conversations produced more lane-keeping errors than passenger conversations
Passenger conversations were worse because passengers gesture and draw the driver's gaze away
Neither conversation type impaired driving relative to silent drives
explain: Phone conversations degraded lane keeping far more than chatting with someone physically present, and phone talk also outstrips listening to the radio or an audiobook in cost. Sustaining a remote conversation appears uniquely draining on the resources driving needs.
hint: One conversation partner shares the driver's situation and can see the road — consider what that changes.

q: A colleague insists that constant juggling of chat, email, and spreadsheets has made him an expert multitasker. Based on task-switching research, what is the most likely reality?
options: Frequent multitaskers tend to show the largest switching costs, so his habit may have made him worse
He is probably right, since research shows switching efficiency improves steadily the more often people juggle tasks in daily life
Switching costs vanish for anyone once the individual tasks become familiar
His overall speed is unchanged, but his accuracy has probably improved
explain: Multitasking usually amounts to rapid task switching, and each switch carries a time cost while the mind reconfigures. Strikingly, the heaviest habitual multitaskers show the biggest switching deficits, so confidence in one's own multitasking is a poor guide to actual performance.
hint: The relationship between how often people juggle tasks and how well they switch is not the intuitive one.

q: Asked to name ink colors, people stumble when the word 'GREEN' appears printed in red ink (Stroop, 1935). What does this interference reveal about skilled reading?
options: Reading requires so much effort that color perception momentarily shuts down
Color and language are processed in the same cortical area, forcing a direct conflict
Years of practice have made word reading automatic — it runs even when it only hurts performance
People habitually value word meanings over colors and choose to read first
explain: The word's identity is processed involuntarily and collides with the color-naming goal, slowing responses. That unstoppable quality is the signature of automaticity: extensively practiced skills come to run with little attentional cost and without deliberate intent (MacLeod, 1991).
hint: Notice that the reading happens despite being completely useless for the task at hand.

q: In multiple-object tracking, viewers follow several highlighted dots as they wander among identical distractors. What does performance on this task suggest about attention?
options: Attention operates strictly on one object at a time, and tracking success relies on guessing
Tracking capacity is effectively unlimited when the objects move slowly enough
People can track only a single moving object unless the objects differ in color
Attention can be split across roughly four or five moving objects at once
explain: Viewers reliably keep tabs on about four to five independently moving targets (Cowan, 2000; Intriligator & Cavanagh, 2001), which argues that attention is not always a single undivided beam. Concurrent tracking of a small set is genuinely possible, though capacity is sharply bounded.
hint: The finding concerns a specific small capacity limit, not an all-or-nothing focus.

q: Keeping your gaze fixed on your laptop, you monitor a coworker approaching in your peripheral vision. What is this ability called?
options: Overt attention
Covert attention
Exogenous capture
Perceptual pop-out
explain: Attending to a location without moving the eyes toward it is covert attention; when gaze and attention travel together, that is overt attention. Covert monitoring lets us keep tabs on locations discreetly and may scout ahead of the eyes to guide where they move next.
hint: The key detail is that the eyes never move while the focus of processing does.

q: In Posner's (1980) cueing procedure, an arrow usually points to where a target will appear, and participants respond without moving their eyes. Targets at correctly cued locations are detected faster than at miscued locations. What does this show?
options: Attention shifted to the cued location ahead of any eye movement, priming processing there in advance
The eyes actually made tiny undetected movements toward the cued location, and these fully explain the speed advantage
Arrow cues improve motor readiness generally, speeding responses to all locations equally
Peripheral vision is sharper than foveal vision whenever a cue is present
explain: Valid cues speed detection even with the eyes pinned to a central cross, so a covert spotlight must have moved to the cued spot and readied processing before the stimulus arrived. If the benefit were general alertness or motor arousal, invalidly cued targets would be detected just as quickly.
hint: Compare correctly cued and miscued targets — a general alerting effect would have helped both equally.

q: Shown a brief, crowded display outside their focus, viewers sometimes report a purple triangle when the display actually contained a purple oval and an orange triangle. Which account explains this error?
options: Late selection — every item's meaning was fully processed, but the response stage mixed up which labels went together
Attenuation — the weakened signal degraded color perception specifically
Perceptual load — spare capacity caused extra features to intrude from the periphery
Feature integration — without focused attention, separately coded features were bound together incorrectly
explain: Treisman's feature-integration theory holds that color, shape, and motion are registered by separate systems and that attention is the glue joining them into unified objects. When attention is absent or rushed, features can recombine wrongly, producing illusory conjunctions like a purple triangle that was never shown.
hint: The individual features were all seen correctly; the mistake lies in how they were put together.

q: One display asks searchers to find a green bar among red bars; another asks for a red tilted bar among red vertical and green tilted bars. As distractors are added to each display, what does feature-integration theory predict?
options: Both searches slow down linearly, since more items always mean more work
Both searches stay equally fast, because color is always processed before orientation
The single-feature search stays fast at any display size, while the conjunction search slows steadily with each added item
The conjunction search becomes fast with practice, while the single-feature search slows steadily as the display grows larger
explain: A target defined by one unique feature pops out preattentively, so display size barely matters. A target defined by a combination of features requires attention to visit items and bind their properties — roughly 20 to 40 milliseconds apiece — so search time climbs linearly with the number of distractors.
hint: One target differs by a single property, the other only by a combination. Which one needs binding?

q: Busy counting how many times jump-ropers in green complete their jumps, many viewers completely miss a costumed figure strolling through the scene. What is this failure called?
options: Simultanagnosia
Inattentional blindness
Visual neglect
Retinal suppression
explain: Missing a fully visible event because attention is engaged elsewhere is inattentional blindness — awareness depends on attention, not just on light reaching the eyes. Neglect and simultanagnosia are attentional disorders that follow brain damage, not everyday failures in healthy viewers.
hint: This happens to perfectly healthy observers whenever attention is absorbed by a demanding count.

q: During a coin trick, observers stared directly at the coin, yet many failed to notice it had been swapped for a different coin (Smith, Lamont, & Henderson, 2012). What does this reveal?
options: Fixating an object does not guarantee attending to it — gaze and awareness can come apart
Foveal vision is too coarse to tell similar coins apart at close range
Memory for coin details is generally poor because those details are almost never relevant to everyday tasks
The motion of the magician's hands masked the retinal image of the swap
explain: Even with the eyes locked on the object, the change went unseen, so overt fixation is not sufficient for awareness — what matters is whether attention is deployed to the relevant properties. Change blindness can strike at the very point of gaze, dissociating looking from seeing.
hint: Everyone's eyes were pointed at the right place; ask what else needed to be pointed there.

q: Volunteers waiting to detect a faint tone show elevated activity in auditory cortex before any sound plays (Leaver et al., 2009). What attentional principle does this illustrate?
options: Activity in sensory cortex is driven purely by stimulation arriving from the sense organs themselves
Auditory areas are always more active than visual areas during rest
Expectation suppresses sensory regions in order to reduce false alarms
Attention prepares relevant sensory regions in advance of an expected stimulus
explain: Goal-driven attention pre-activates the cortical territory that will process an anticipated input, effectively warming up the relevant machinery before anything arrives. This readying function helps explain why attended and expected stimuli are detected faster and more reliably than unexpected ones.
hint: The activity appears before the stimulus exists — ask what could switch it on that early.

q: While people awaited moving dots after a directional cue, fMRI showed activity in the intraparietal sulcus — a region not needed for motion analysis itself — alongside motion-sensitive area MT (Shulman et al., 1999). What role does this suggest for the parietal region?
options: It performs a slower backup computation of the dots' motion in case area MT fails to register it
It acts as a controller, directing which sensory regions get amplified for the current goal
It stores the memory of the arrow cue until the response can be made
It generates the eye movements needed to pursue the moving dots
explain: Since the intraparietal sulcus does not compute motion, its activity during anticipation points to a supervisory job: posterior parietal cortex modulates other regions, turning up areas like MT that the current goal requires. Attention here is the control of processing rather than the processing itself.
hint: The region is active for a computation it cannot perform — ask what job that leaves for it.

q: Weak electrical stimulation of a monkey's frontal eye fields — too weak to trigger an eye movement — improves the animal's detection of targets at the corresponding spot in space (Moore & Fallah, 2001). What is the significance of this finding?
options: The frontal eye fields are purely motor structures whose only job is moving the eyes
Detection improved only because the stimulation caused the eyes to drift slightly and imperceptibly toward the target location
Circuitry that plans eye movements can also allocate covert attention to a location without any movement occurring
Stimulation raised overall arousal, improving detection everywhere in the visual field
explain: Subthreshold stimulation produced a spatially specific perceptual benefit at exactly the location that site would have moved the eyes toward, with no movement occurring. This ties overt and covert orienting to shared machinery: the same retinotopic eye-movement map can boost perception at a spot it merely points to.
hint: The improvement was confined to one location and the eyes never moved — combine those two facts.

q: Deep in goal-driven search for your black car in a parking lot, a firework bursts overhead and yanks your attention skyward. Which neural arrangement fits this capture by an unexpected event?
options: A largely right-hemisphere network including the temporoparietal junction responds to salient, unexpected stimuli
The same dorsal goal-directed parietal network that guides deliberate search also handles all interruptions from the environment
Primary visual cortex reorients attention on its own, without any network involvement
The frontal lobes shut down sensory processing until the search goal is complete
explain: Corbetta and Shulman (2002) distinguish a dorsal, goal-directed system centered on posterior parietal cortex from a stimulus-driven system lateralized to the right hemisphere, including the temporoparietal junction, that flags unexpected salient events. The firework engages the latter, interrupting ongoing goal-driven search.
hint: Two partly separate systems exist — one for goals you set yourself, one for surprises from the world.

q: After a stroke damaging the right parietal lobe, patients often neglect the entire left visual field, yet comparable damage to the left parietal lobe rarely produces neglect of the right field. What explains this asymmetry?
options: Language areas in the left hemisphere assume control of spatial attention whenever the left parietal lobe is damaged
The left visual field receives a weaker cortical representation than the right in all healthy brains
Neglect only ever appears when both parietal lobes are damaged simultaneously
The right parietal lobe can generate attention in both visual fields, so it compensates when the left is damaged
explain: The left parietal lobe directs attention only to the right visual field, while the right parietal lobe covers both fields. When the left lobe is damaged, the intact right lobe pitches in for the right field — but nothing backs up the right lobe, so its loss leaves the left field unattended.
hint: Ask which hemisphere's parietal lobe holds a map of both sides of space rather than just one.

q: What is memory?
options: Using past information to support cognition in the present
Holding sensory input unchanged until it reaches long-term storage
Repeating current information without accessing anything from the past
Recording every experience permanently in the nervous system
explain: Memory is the use of information obtained in the past to generate some cognitive function in the present.
hint: The definition links past information to present cognition.

q: A stimulus is initially processed so that it becomes represented in the nervous system. Which memory process is this?
options: Retrieval
Encoding
Storage
Rehearsal
explain: Encoding is the initial processing that represents information in the nervous system. If information is never encoded, it cannot later be remembered.
hint: This is the entry step, not maintenance or access.

q: Which memory process means that encoded information remains represented beyond immediate processing?
options: Attention
Retrieval
Storage
Chunking
explain: Storage means that information encoded by the nervous system remains encoded in some form for longer than immediate processing.
hint: Ask which process keeps an encoding available over time.

q: You deliberately bring a stored phone number back into awareness so you can dial it. Which process is illustrated?
options: Encoding the number
Storing the number
Rehearsing the number
Retrieving the number
explain: Retrieval is cognitively accessing stored information for a purpose, such as using a remembered number.
hint: The information is already stored; the task is to access it.

q: Researchers compare two memory systems by asking how much each can hold and how long information remains available. Which pair of measures are they using?
options: Capacity and duration
Encoding and retrieval
Accuracy and rehearsal
Attention and interference
explain: Capacity and duration are the two major behavioral measures used to compare memory systems.
hint: One measure is about amount; the other is about time.

q: Which sequence lists the three memory systems in the Atkinson-Shiffrin modal model?
options: Encoding, storage, retrieval
Sensory, short-term, and long-term memory
Phonological loop, sketchpad, central executive
Visual memory, auditory memory, episodic memory
explain: Atkinson and Shiffrin's 1968 modal model proposes sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory, each with its own capacity and duration.
hint: Choose the sequence that moves from initial sensory retention to temporary and then durable storage.

q: In the modal-model diagram, which set of transitions is correctly matched with its process?
options: Sensory input to sensory memory by retrieval; STM to LTM by attention
Sensory memory to STM by encoding; LTM to STM by rehearsal
Attention to STM; encoding to LTM; retrieval back to STM
Sensory memory to LTM by attention; LTM to STM by maintenance
explain: The diagram shows attention moving selected sensory information into STM, encoding moving STM information into LTM, and retrieval bringing LTM information back into STM.
hint: Trace the arrows in both directions around short-term memory.

q: What was a major contribution of the modal model?
options: It treated all remembering as one storage process
It rejected any role for long-term memory
It explained memory only through brain anatomy
It separated current STM from durable LTM
explain: The model articulated different storage roles: short-term memory for current tasks and long-term memory for extended storage.
hint: Focus on the distinction between working with information now and retaining it later.

q: Which observation best illustrates why capacity and duration must be treated as separate properties?
options: One system can be brief and limited; another long-lasting and large
Any system with a large capacity must also encode information more quickly
A system's duration is determined entirely by how accurately it retrieves
All memory systems have equal capacity but differ only in sensory modality
explain: Limited short-term capacity contrasts with much larger long-term capacity, and brief retention contrasts with memories that can last a lifetime. Amount and time therefore describe different properties.
hint: One property answers 'how much'; the other answers 'how long.'

q: What is the primary function of sensory memory in the modal model?
options: To rehearse information until it becomes permanent
To briefly retain information just encoded by the sensory organs
To combine visual and auditory information with long-term memory
To retrieve facts that have already entered long-term memory
explain: Sensory memory briefly stores information immediately after sensory encoding.
hint: It is the first, very brief holding stage after sensation.

q: Why does the modal model include sensory memory before short-term memory?
options: It converts all input directly into lifelong memories
It prevents attention from selecting any information
It briefly holds input for selection into STM
It replaces the need for encoding and retrieval
explain: Sensory memory keeps a rapidly fading trace available long enough for attention to select information for short-term memory.
hint: Its purpose is to create a brief selection window.

q: You look at a scene, close your eyes, and can momentarily experience the whole image before it fades. This is an example of:
options: Long-term retrieval
Maintenance rehearsal
The episodic buffer
A brief sensory trace
explain: A momentary visual trace after the scene disappears illustrates the brief persistence of information in sensory memory.
hint: The experience is vivid but disappears rapidly.

q: In Sperling's whole-report condition, what were participants asked to do after viewing three rows of letters?
options: Report the whole grid as fully as possible
Report only the row indicated by a later tone
Count backward by threes before reporting
Judge whether a second display had changed
explain: Whole-report participants tried to report as many letters as possible from the entire grid.
hint: The condition name tells you the scope of the requested report.

q: What distinguished Sperling's partial-report condition from whole report?
options: Participants saw only one row rather than three rows
A high, medium, or low tone selected the report row
Participants rehearsed the grid before seeing the cue
A visual arrow selected a letter before the grid appeared
explain: After the letter grid disappeared, an auditory tone indicated the high, middle, or low row that participants should report.
hint: The crucial cue came after the display and selected one row.

q: Sperling found roughly 25% recall in whole report but 75-80% of the cued row in partial report. What conclusion follows?
options: Participants encoded only the top row of every display
The tone transferred letters directly into long-term memory
A broad sensory trace briefly supported the cued report
Whole report measured a larger sensory capacity than partial report
explain: High partial-report accuracy indicates that much of the grid was briefly available in sensory memory, even though the trace faded before all letters could be reported.
hint: The cue arrived after the grid vanished, yet participants could access any indicated row.

q: Why did whole-report participants usually produce letters from only one row despite having briefly seen the entire grid?
options: Only one row ever reached the sensory organs
The other rows were stored permanently but could not be retrieved
The auditory cue actively erased two of the rows
The trace faded while the first row was being reported
explain: The display was broadly available for a moment, but reporting takes time. By the time one row was spoken, the remaining sensory information had largely faded.
hint: Separate how much was briefly available from how much could be reported before it disappeared.

q: What happened when Sperling increased the delay between the letter display and the row-indicating tone?
options: Recall declined as the cue delay increased
Recall improved because participants had more rehearsal time
Recall stayed constant across all cue delays
Recall shifted from sensory memory directly to LTM
explain: Longer delays produced fewer recalled letters. The shorter the delay between display and tone, the more of the sensory trace remained available.
hint: Consider what happens to a rapidly fading trace while the cue is delayed.

q: Which result would most directly contradict the interpretation of a rapidly fading sensory store?
options: Whole report remains lower than immediate partial report
Partial-report accuracy stays high after a long cue delay
Immediate tones allow participants to report the selected row
Participants retain a visual trace briefly after the display ends
explain: If partial-report accuracy stayed equally high despite a long delay, the trace would not appear to fade rapidly. The actual result was declining recall with longer delays.
hint: Look for a finding that removes the effect of elapsed time on the sensory trace.

q: In the modal model, what does short-term memory primarily store?
options: All sensory input, whether attended or not
Only information retrieved from long-term memory
Attended information selected from sensory memory
Permanent knowledge accumulated across the lifespan
explain: Short-term memory stores information selected by attention from sensory memory, typically for about 15-30 seconds unless it is rehearsed.
hint: Attention controls the handoff from the first memory stage.

q: Why might someone repeat a newly heard phone number while preparing to save it?
options: To move it backward into sensory memory
To prevent any neural encoding of the digits
To reduce the number of meaningful chunks
To keep it active in STM for later encoding
explain: Repetition keeps information active in short-term memory so it remains available for use or encoding.
hint: The repetition protects temporary information from being lost immediately.

q: What auditory short-term-memory capacity did Miller's 1956 work emphasize?
options: About 7 plus or minus 2 items
Exactly 4 visual objects
About 15 seconds of speech
An unlimited number of letters
explain: Across lists of letters, numbers, and words, Miller found an average auditory STM span of about 7 plus or minus 2 items.
hint: Recall the famous stable span estimate.

q: How did Miller assess auditory STM capacity in the study described?
options: Participants matched two pictures after a delay
Participants repeated ordered verbal lists in sequence
Participants recalled a cued row from a letter grid
Participants counted backward while retaining a trigram
explain: Miller presented ordered lists of verbal items and asked participants to repeat them in order, revealing a stable individual span.
hint: This was a span task using ordered verbal material.

q: In the visual change-detection task, what must a participant decide?
options: Which row a tone identifies
Whether a spoken item was a noun
Whether the second display matched the first
Whether an image belongs in long-term memory
explain: Participants view objects such as colored squares, then judge whether the next display matches or contains a changed property.
hint: The task compares a first display with a second display.

q: What capacity estimate do visual short-term-memory change-detection results suggest?
options: One item regardless of stimulus type
Seven to nine complex objects
Fifteen to thirty visual items
Roughly four to five items
explain: The plotted change-detection data suggest that visual STM holds approximately four to five items.
hint: The visual estimate is smaller than Miller's auditory 7 plus or minus 2.

q: What is a chunk?
options: Elements combined into one meaningful whole
Any single sensory feature before attention selects it
An irrelevant item that displaces an older memory
A neural response that occurs only during retrieval
explain: A chunk is a combination of letters, numbers, or sounds that is treated as one meaningful unit.
hint: Meaning allows multiple elements to count as one unit.

q: Why is '1776 1492 2001 2018' easier to retain than the unspaced string '1776149220012018' for someone who recognizes the years?
options: Spacing increases sensory-memory duration
Known years turn several digits into larger chunks
The spaced version contains fewer physical digits
The unspaced version cannot enter the nervous system
explain: Recognizable years let long-term knowledge organize many digits into a few meaningful chunks, reducing the number of STM units.
hint: The amount of ink is unchanged; the number of meaningful units changes.

q: What does effective chunking depend on?
options: A larger sensory-memory duration than other people
The absence of any previously learned patterns
LTM for previously learned meaningful patterns
A central executive that stores every detail permanently
explain: Chunking draws on long-term memory, where familiar patterns and combinations are represented, so multiple elements can be grouped as a unit.
hint: You can group a pattern only if the pattern already means something to you.

q: Why can a professional mnemonist appear to have a 'super-memory' for long strings?
options: Their sensory organs encode more kinds of input
Their STM holds an unlimited number of unrelated items
They avoid using long-term memory while recalling
They combine many elements into larger chunks
explain: The apparent super-memory of professional mnemonists reflects skilled chunk formation, not an expanded basic STM capacity.
hint: The advantage changes how items are organized, not the underlying item limit.

q: What pattern in Chase and Simon's 1973 chess study best supports a chunking explanation of expertise?
options: Experts led for game positions, but much less for random positions
Experts and novices performed equally for game positions, but experts led for random boards
Experts recalled all boards perfectly because their visual STM was unlimited
Novices outperformed experts whenever pieces formed meaningful configurations
explain: Experts could use familiar game configurations as meaningful chunks. Random arrangements removed much of that structure, sharply reducing their advantage.
hint: Expertise helps most when the arrangement contains patterns learned through experience.

q: The resource-pool figure showed capacity falling from simple colored squares to Chinese characters, random polygons, and shaded cubes. What principle does this pattern illustrate?
options: Visual STM always holds exactly seven items
Complex items use more of a limited STM resource
Only familiar stimuli can ever enter visual STM
Stimulus complexity affects duration but never capacity
explain: The figure treats capacity as a limited pool: simple colored squares permit more items, whereas structurally complex objects consume more resources per item.
hint: Compare how much processing each object demands, not just how many objects appear.

q: How long can information theoretically remain in short-term memory if it is continuously rehearsed?
options: Only about one second
Exactly fifteen seconds
While rehearsal continues
Only until a sensory cue appears
explain: STM can theoretically last forever as long as rehearsal keeps reactivating the initial encoding.
hint: Rehearsal changes the usual duration limit.

q: What is rehearsal?
options: Selecting one sensory row with an auditory tone
Grouping familiar elements into meaningful units
Retrieving a permanent fact from long-term memory
Repeating STM content to reactivate encoding
explain: Rehearsal is the repetition of information in STM, which reactivates the initial encoding and maintains availability.
hint: It is an active repetition process within temporary memory.

q: What was the purpose of counting backward by threes in the Brown-Peterson task?
options: To block rehearsal during the trigram delay
To increase the number of chunks in the trigram
To transfer the trigram into sensory memory
To measure visual change detection
explain: After receiving a three-letter trigram, participants counted backward by threes so they could not rehearse the letters while waiting to report them.
hint: The secondary task occupies the process that would maintain the letters.

q: What duration of unrehearsed STM did the Peterson distraction results suggest?
options: About one second
About fifteen seconds
About one minute
An unlimited duration
explain: Recall declined steeply under distraction, leading to an estimate of roughly fifteen seconds for STM without rehearsal.
hint: It is shorter than the modal model's broad 15-30 second range.

q: Which explanation says forgetting occurs simply because time passes?
options: Retrieval failure
Chunking
Decay
Interference
explain: Decay attributes forgetting to the passage of time, whereas interference attributes it to competing information.
hint: No competing material is required by this account.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes proactive from retroactive interference?
options: Proactive affects the past; retroactive affects only sensory input
Proactive is time-based decay; retroactive is failed encoding
Proactive protects new learning; retroactive protects old learning
Earlier disrupts new learning; later disrupts old learning
explain: Proactive interference carries forward from earlier information to disrupt later learning, while retroactive interference comes from newer information and disrupts older material.
hint: Think forward for proactive and backward for retroactive.

q: Why was Peterson et al.'s original decay interpretation later questioned?
options: Prior trigrams could proactively disrupt the current one
Participants were allowed unlimited rehearsal on every trial
The experiment measured only long-term autobiographical memory
The trigram was always replaced by a visual square
explain: Across repeated trials, previously studied trigrams could accumulate and proactively interfere with the current one, so time was not the only changing factor.
hint: Consider what builds up as participants complete many trigrams.

q: What did Keppel and Underwood's 1962 reanalysis find on the earliest Brown-Peterson trials?
options: Recall was already near zero at the shortest delay
Early trials retained trigrams across fifteen seconds
Longer delays consistently improved recall accuracy
Only retroactive interference occurred on the first trial
explain: On the first few trials, before many prior trigrams could interfere, recall stayed relatively high across delays up to about fifteen seconds.
hint: Early trials minimize the buildup of prior material.

q: What conclusion did the Keppel and Underwood pattern support once later trials were also considered?
options: Only rehearsal explains every forgetting effect
Neither time nor prior material matters for STM
STM loss can reflect decay and interference
Sensory memory is the sole source of forgetting
explain: Good early-trial retention implicated proactive interference in much of the original curve, while decay appearing on later trials left room for both processes.
hint: The reanalysis did not reduce forgetting to a single cause.

q: In Lewandowsky et al. (2004), why did participants repeatedly say an irrelevant word aloud while recalling letters?
options: To increase similarity among the letter strings
To provide an auditory cue for the correct response
To place the letters into long-term memory
To block rehearsal without adding competing letters
explain: The irrelevant repeated word created articulatory suppression, intended to block rehearsal while avoiding the buildup of competing letter information in STM.
hint: The manipulation isolates time by blocking silent repetition.

q: Lewandowsky et al. varied how quickly participants recalled letters but found no recall difference across speeds. What conclusion did they draw?
options: Time alone caused no decay without interference
Faster recall always creates stronger proactive interference
Articulatory suppression extends sensory memory indefinitely
Letter recall depends entirely on visual change detection
explain: If more elapsed time alone caused decay, slower responding should have reduced recall. Because response speed had no effect, they argued that time alone did not cause forgetting.
hint: Ask what should have happened in the slower condition if pure decay were operating.

q: What core change did Baddeley's 1974 working-memory model make to the idea of STM?
options: It divided memory only by how long traces last
It made STM an active workspace for manipulating information
It removed visual and auditory processing from temporary memory
It defined STM as a passive container with no task role
explain: Baddeley challenged passive-storage accounts and described working memory as an active workspace for holding and manipulating information during a task.
hint: The key contrast is passive storage versus active mental work.

q: Which working-memory component would be most directly engaged when mentally rotating a remembered object?
options: Phonological loop
Long-term store
Visual sketchpad
Sensory register
explain: The visuo-spatial sketchpad holds visual information while allowing it to be analyzed and manipulated, as in mental rotation.
hint: The task requires visual-spatial manipulation, not verbal repetition.

q: Which working-memory component repeats auditory information so it can be used or analyzed?
options: Episodic buffer
Central executive
Visual sketchpad
Phonological loop
explain: The phonological loop is the auditory component of working memory and supports repetition of auditory information.
hint: Choose the component specialized for speech-like or auditory material.

q: What is the central executive's basic role in the working-memory model?
options: Coordinate the stores and control entry into WM
Store visual patterns permanently without attention
Repeat only spoken information during a delay
Preserve every sensory trace for about one second
explain: The central executive coordinates between the visuo-spatial sketchpad and phonological loop and acts as a gatekeeper for information entering working memory.
hint: It manages the specialized stores rather than serving as one of them.

q: What hypothesis did Brooks (1968) test by pairing verbal or visual memory with verbal or pointing responses?
options: Whether rehearsal transfers every STM item into LTM
Whether visual and auditory buffers are separate
Whether sensory memory lasts longer for tones than pictures
Whether chess expertise expands visual STM capacity
explain: Brooks compared verbal and visual memory tasks with different response modes to test whether the two buffers were separate and whether one mode interfered with the matching memory task.
hint: The design crosses the modality of the memory with the modality of the response.

q: In Brooks's visual-memory task, participants followed the corners of a block letter and judged whether each point was extreme. Which response produced the largest slowdown?
options: Silently rehearsing the word 'shoe'
Saying whether each point was a noun
Pointing to answers on a visual grid
Reporting a row selected by a tone
explain: The visual task was much slower with a pointing response on a visual grid, consistent with competition within a visual processing code.
hint: The biggest cost came when memory and response used the same visual-spatial channel.

q: What is the episodic buffer?
options: A permanent visual store outside executive control
A rehearsal loop limited to spoken information
A sensory trace that fades before attention acts
A brief store binding visual, auditory, and LTM
explain: The episodic buffer combines information from the phonological loop, visual sketchpad, and long-term memory into time-based multisensory representations.
hint: Its defining job is integration across otherwise separate stores.

q: Which statement correctly describes control and awareness in the episodic-buffer account?
options: The executive controls it; it supports conscious multisensory episodes
The phonological loop controls it, and its contents never reach awareness
Long-term memory controls it without any working-memory involvement
Sensory memory controls it only during visual perception
explain: The episodic buffer is controlled by the central executive and is proposed to support conscious awareness of integrated, time-based, multisensory memories.
hint: Link the system manager with the store that binds information into an episode.

q: Why does the working-memory model distinguish auditory and visual stores?
options: Both modalities are stored with one identical code
The modalities use distinct, separately processed codes
Only auditory information can be manipulated during a task
Visual information bypasses working memory entirely
explain: Brooks's results argue that visual and auditory information rely on distinct memory codes and can be processed separately.
hint: Separate buffers predict different patterns of modality-specific interference.

q: Some individual differences in STM capacity may reflect differences in:
options: Sensory exposure duration
Long-term storage size
Filtering irrelevant information from working memory
The number of sensory organs engaged during the memory task
explain: Higher-capacity individuals may be better at preventing irrelevant material from consuming limited working-memory resources.
hint: Capacity can depend on what the gatekeeper keeps out.

q: In Vogel et al. (2005), what did the red rectangles do in the critical visual STM trials?
options: They identified the side participants should ignore
They replaced the blue targets during the delay
They served as the only items participants had to remember
They were irrelevant distractors beside two blue targets
explain: Participants were to remember two blue rectangles while two red rectangles appeared as irrelevant distractors. The task tested whether those distractors entered working memory.
hint: The blue items were targets; the other color tested filtering.
