explain: Aphantasia names the absence of voluntary visual imagery; congenital cases have simply never had a working mind's eye. Zeman's surveys put its prevalence around one to three percent — uncommon, but far from vanishingly rare.
hint: The prefix signals absence, and the condition is rarer than one in twenty.

q: People with aphantasia score at the floor on the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire, yet Keogh and Pearson (2018) found their performance on spatial tasks like paper folding is typical. What does this dissociation suggest?
options: Questionnaires like the VVIQ are too subjective to measure anything real
Aphantasia reflects a cautious reporting style rather than any genuine underlying difference in imagery
Object imagery and spatial imagery are served by at least partly distinct systems
Spatial tasks are solved verbally by everyone, imagers and non-imagers alike
explain: If a single imagery faculty existed, losing vivid object imagery should drag spatial manipulation down with it. Instead the two abilities come apart — no pictured objects, yet normal mental folding — pointing to separable systems for object appearance and spatial transformation.
hint: One ability is missing while the other is untouched — what architecture allows that?

q: A five-year-old announces 'My sock puppet is mayor of the moon' — a sentence nobody has ever produced — and listeners understand it instantly. A honeybee's waggle dance, by contrast, can only ever encode a food source's direction and distance. Which design feature of language does the child show and the bee lack?
options: Arbitrariness — the sound of a word has no natural link to its meaning
Displacement — the ability to refer to things not physically present
Generativity — a finite vocabulary combines into unlimited novel messages
Prosody — patterns of stress and intonation that add meaning beyond the words themselves
explain: Generativity (also called productivity or digital infinity) lets speakers recombine a fixed stock of words under grammatical rules into an endless supply of brand-new sentences. Chomsky (1991) described language as "digital and infinite"; no animal signal system, including the bee dance's fixed direction-and-distance code, shows this open-ended combinatorial power.
hint: Focus on what lets a limited word list yield sentences never spoken before.

q: Ouattara et al. (2009) showed that male Campbell's monkeys chain calls such as 'boom boom' and 'krak-oo' into ordered sequences, where the order itself changes the warning conveyed. Why do most researchers still classify this as proto-syntax rather than true language?
options: The repertoire is a small, fixed set of messages — the calls never combine into open-ended novel meanings
Vocal signals cannot in principle carry syntactic structure, so the sequences must be reflexive
The sequences vary randomly between individuals, so the ordering carries no shared meaning
The monkeys produce these sequences only around human observers, so the behavior is an artifact of training rather than natural communication
explain: Ordered call combinations are impressive, but the whole system tops out at a handful of distinct messages tied to immediate events like predators. Human syntax, by contrast, generates an effectively unlimited set of novel sentences from tens of thousands of words — a difference of kind, not just degree.
hint: Ask how many distinct messages the whole call system can ever express.

q: Over dinner, a friend relives a blizzard she survived a decade ago and sketches plans for next summer's trip. Her dog, meanwhile, can only signal present-moment states like hunger or alarm. Which design feature of language accounts for the difference?
options: Generativity, since her stories combine words in novel ways
Arbitrariness, since the word 'blizzard' bears no natural resemblance to actual snow
Prosody, since her intonation conveys the drama of the storm
Displacement, the capacity to refer to things absent from the here and now
explain: Displacement is the power to communicate about the spatially and temporally absent — past storms, future trips, hypothetical events. Animal signals overwhelmingly announce what is happening right now, which is why a dog can beg for dinner but cannot reminisce about last winter.
hint: Notice when the events she describes are actually happening.

q: Alex the African Grey parrot used over 200 spoken labels, including abstract ones like color and shape (Pepperberg), and Washoe the chimpanzee learned roughly 250 signs, even coining 'dirty good' for toilet. What ceiling ultimately kept researchers from crediting either animal with genuine language?
options: Their labels never generalized beyond the specific training objects they were taught with
Neither ever produced novel sentences with grammatical structure beyond short fixed combinations
Both responded only when food rewards were offered, showing conditioning rather than genuine communication
Both lost their vocabularies within months once daily training sessions ended
explain: Vocabulary was never the sticking point — productivity was. Despite years of training, Alex stayed at two-word combinations like 'blue square,' and Washoe never strung signs into novel, grammatically organized sentences. Generating unlimited new constructions from fixed symbols remains, so far, uniquely human.
hint: Both animals amassed big vocabularies — think about how far their combining went.

q: Two ants from the same colony meet along a trail and touch each other with their mouths and antennae. Researchers know they are actually exchanging chemical signals that can convey, for instance, whether food was found along the path. What are these chemicals called?
options: Pheromones — chemical messengers passed between members of the same species
Neurotransmitters — chemicals released across synapses within an individual's nervous system
Hormones — chemicals carried through an individual's bloodstream to regulate its own organs
Morphemes — the smallest units of a signal that carry meaning on their own
explain: Ants pass information through pheromones, chemicals transferred between individuals that can signal things like the presence of a food source along a path. Neurotransmitters and hormones operate inside a single organism's own body, and morphemes are units of human language, not chemicals.
hint: These chemicals travel between animals, not within one body.

q: One account holds that children build language through imitation and reinforcement, like any other skill; a rival account holds that children arrive pre-equipped with grammatical scaffolding, needing input only to fill in local details. Which pairing correctly matches theorist to position?
options: Chomsky — reinforcement learning; Skinner — universal grammar
Skinner — reinforcement learning; Chomsky — universal grammar
Whorf — reinforcement learning; Sapir — universal grammar
Saffran — reinforcement learning; Pepperberg — universal grammar
explain: Skinner's Verbal Behavior treated language as operant learning shaped by reward and modeling, while Chomsky countered that a universal grammar — innate structural scaffolding shared by all languages — comes first, with experience supplying only local details like which words and which word orders.
hint: One of these names is famous for behaviorism, the other for nativism.

q: Children reliably transform 'The boy who is eating is holding the bear' into a question by moving the correct 'is' — a structure-sensitive rule they were never taught and that simple examples cannot settle. Chomsky cited such cases as evidence for what argument?
options: Late closure — children attach new words to the phrase currently being processed
Statistical learning — children track which auxiliary verbs co-occur most often
Poverty of the stimulus — input alone is too thin to fix the grammar children acquire
Child-directed speech — exaggerated parental input teaches the question rule directly
explain: The examples children hear are compatible with a simpler but wrong rule (move the first 'is'), yet children essentially never make that error. Chomsky's poverty-of-the-stimulus argument holds that when the data underdetermine the grammar, the missing constraints must come from innate structural knowledge.
hint: The key is that the available examples cannot decide between two rules.

q: Adults who migrate late often plateau at a simplified pidgin, yet their children spontaneously develop a creole with full grammar no one modeled for them; deaf children with no sign input likewise invent structured gesture systems (Goldin-Meadow et al., 1984). Why do nativists lean on these cases?
options: They show children imitate their peers more faithfully than their parents
They show that reinforcement schedules simply operate more efficiently in childhood than adulthood
They show any species can build grammar when immersion is total enough
They show grammar emerging even when the environment offers no adequate model
explain: In both cases the output outstrips the input: creole-speaking children impose consistent grammar their pidgin-speaking parents never supplied, and isolated deaf children generate structure from nothing. Contrast that with intensively trained apes who never do — the asymmetry points to a species-specific, possibly innate capacity to acquire language even without adequate input.
hint: Compare what these children produce with what they were actually given.

q: Saffran, Aslin, and Newport (1996) played 8-month-olds a few minutes of a continuous synthetic stream like 'bidakupadotigolabu,' where syllables within a 'word' always co-occurred but syllables spanning word boundaries rarely did. What did the infants' listening behavior reveal?
options: They oriented longer to boundary-spanning sequences, showing they had tracked syllable co-occurrence statistics
They oriented longer to the trained words, showing an innate preference for familiar lexical units over new ones
They showed no preference at all, showing that segmentation requires audible pauses between individual words
They responded only when the stream was recorded in exaggerated sing-song motherese, showing that prosody alone drives early segmentation
explain: Novelty preference did the work: infants oriented longer toward part-words whose syllable transitions had been rare, treating the statistically coherent sequences as familiar 'words.' A few minutes of exposure was enough to extract transition probabilities — powerful evidence that statistical learning helps crack the segmentation problem.
hint: Babies tend to find the statistically unfamiliar item more interesting.

q: Liu, Kuhl, and Tsao found that infants' speech-sound discrimination tracked their mothers' use of stretched, exaggerated vowels, yet Ochs (1982) documented Samoan communities where adults rarely address pre-linguistic children — and those children become fluent anyway. What is the best synthesis?
options: Child-directed speech is necessary for typical language development but not sufficient on its own
Child-directed speech can speed acquisition, but children can also learn by observing others' speech
Vowel exaggeration helps early perception while conversational overhearing builds only vocabulary, never grammar
Cultural differences in parenting produce corresponding differences in final adult language competence
explain: Motherese correlates with sharper early speech discrimination, so it likely gives a boost — but the Samoan case shows direct infant-directed talk is not required. Children immersed in ambient language reach fluency by observation, which is why researchers treat child-directed speech as an accelerant, not a prerequisite.
hint: One study shows a benefit; the other shows what happens without it.

q: The word 'apples' splits into 'apple' plus an '-s' signaling plurality, each piece carrying meaning; 'apple' itself cannot be divided further without losing meaning altogether. What are these smallest meaningful units of language called?
options: Phonemes, the smallest sound units that can change a word's meaning
Graphemes, the written characters that map onto individual speech sounds
Morphemes, the smallest units of speech that carry meaning on their own
Syllables, the rhythmic beats into which spoken words naturally divide
explain: Morphemes are meaning-bearing atoms: 'apple' is one, and the plural '-s' is another because it contributes meaning (more than one). Phonemes, by contrast, are sound atoms — 'apple' contains several phonemes but only one morpheme, since no smaller chunk of it means anything.
hint: The question is about units of meaning, not units of sound.

q: Warren (1970) excised the 's' from a word in a recorded sentence and spliced a cough into the gap. Listeners insisted the sentence was intact, and even those who noticed the cough could not say which sound it had replaced. What does this phonemic restoration effect demonstrate?
options: Top-down expectations fill in missing speech sounds, so we hear phonemes that were never present
A cough shares enough acoustic energy with fricatives that the ear cannot separate the two sources
Attention narrows under listening load, causing brief nonspeech noises to go completely undetected
Auditory memory stores sentences as whole units, erasing any record of individual missing phonemes
explain: The surrounding sentence generates a strong prediction about which phoneme belongs in the gap, and perception obliges — listeners genuinely hear the absent 's.' Like visual completion of occluded objects, it shows speech perception is a constructive process blending signal with expectation, not a passive recording.
hint: Think about what the rest of the sentence lets listeners predict.

q: A video shows a face articulating 'ga' while the soundtrack plays 'ba.' With eyes open, most viewers hear 'da'; with eyes closed, the same clip suddenly sounds like 'ba' (McGurk & MacDonald, 1976). What is the best interpretation?
options: Vision completely overrides audition whenever the two channels conflict during speech
The illusion reflects response bias — people report a compromise sound just to resolve their uncertainty
Lip-reading is a deliberate strategy that listeners switch on only when audio quality degrades
Speech perception automatically fuses visual articulation cues with the acoustic signal
explain: 'Da' is neither what the mouth showed nor what the speaker said — it is a fusion the brain computes from conflicting visual and auditory evidence. The effect is involuntary and persists even when you know the trick, showing lip information feeds speech perception continuously, not just when sound is missing.
hint: The reported sound matches neither input — ask where 'da' came from.

q: Spoken aloud, 'I scream' and 'ice cream' are nearly indistinguishable, and waveform recordings show that talkers rarely pause between words at all. Which core challenge of speech comprehension does this illustrate?
options: Lexical ambiguity — a single word form carries several unrelated meanings
Segmentation — finding word boundaries in a continuous acoustic stream
Parsing — assigning each word its grammatical role within the sentence
Prosodic ambiguity — stress patterns fail to distinguish the two phrases
explain: There are no reliable silences marking where one word ends and the next begins — the signal runs together, and multiple segmentations can fit the same sounds. Listeners solve it with cues like syllable statistics and context; that is why identical acoustics can land as a dessert or a shriek.
hint: The problem is deciding where one word stops and the next starts.

q: Participants hear 'The garden was filled with spiders and other bugs' and, at the exact moment 'bugs' arrives, judge letter strings in a lexical decision task. Within the first 200 milliseconds, which probe words showed speeded responses in Swinney (1979)?
options: Only 'ant' — the sentence context suppressed the espionage sense before it could activate
Only 'spy' — low-frequency meanings are checked first precisely because they are unexpected
Both 'ant' and 'spy' — all meanings of the homophone were briefly activated despite context
Neither word — semantic priming from spoken sentences requires at least a full second to build
explain: For a brief window, the mind opens every file on an ambiguous word: probes related to both the insect and the espionage senses were faster, even though the sentence pointed only to insects. By roughly 200 milliseconds the context-inappropriate meaning is pruned — selection happens after exhaustive access, not instead of it.
hint: The timing matters — this probe landed before context had time to prune.

q: Readers stumble over 'The man who whistles tunes pianos,' initially bundling 'tunes' into the subject phrase 'the man who whistles tunes' and then crashing when 'pianos' arrives. Which parsing principle predicts exactly this garden-path error?
options: Late closure — new words are attached to the phrase currently being processed
Backward inference — earlier material is reinterpreted using later information
Phonemic restoration — an expected relative pronoun gets perceptually filled in
Frequency bias — 'tunes' occurs more often as a noun, so that reading wins the race
explain: Late closure says the parser keeps the current phrase open and hangs each incoming word on it as long as grammar allows. Attaching 'tunes' to 'the man who whistles' is grammatically legal, so readers do it — and are then stranded when 'pianos' cannot serve as the sentence's verb, forcing a full reparse.
hint: Which principle concerns where incoming words get attached?

q: Trueswell et al. (1994) eye-tracked people reading 'The defendant examined by the lawyer...' versus 'The evidence examined by the lawyer...'. Regressive re-reading clustered on the defendant version. If parsing were driven by syntax alone, what should have happened instead, and what does the result show?
options: Only the evidence version should mislead, showing rare words trigger reanalysis
Regressive eye movements should disappear in both versions, showing that passive constructions never produce garden paths
The defendant version should read faster, showing animate subjects ease parsing
Both versions should mislead equally, so the difference shows word meaning guides parsing immediately
explain: Syntactically the two sentences are twins, so a syntax-first parser should garden-path both. Readers did not: because evidence cannot plausibly examine anything, they never built the doomed 'the evidence examined...' reading. Semantics was consulted during the first pass, not afterward — a problem for strict syntax-first accounts.
hint: The two sentences share identical structure — only plausibility differs.

q: You read: 'Dana promised Marcus she would water his plants. She forgot within a week.' Deciding that 'she' in the second sentence refers to Dana rather than Marcus — or anyone else — is an example of what?
options: Causal inference, linking an earlier event to a later consequence
Anaphoric inference, mapping a pronoun onto its earlier antecedent
Instrumental inference, supplying the unstated tool used for a task
Elaborative inference, adding expected details beyond the given text
explain: An anaphor is an expression — often a pronoun — that points back to something already introduced, its antecedent. Nothing in 'she' itself picks out Dana; the reader computes the link from gender, structure, and plausibility. Discourse would collapse without these constant, silent antecedent assignments.
hint: The job here is figuring out who a pronoun points back to.

q: Haviland and Clark (1974) had people self-pace through either 'Mary got the picnic supplies out of the car' or 'Mary got the beer out of the car,' each followed by 'The beer was warm.' Which result emerged, and why?
options: The second sentence was faster after 'picnic supplies,' since a general category primes many nouns at once
Reading times were identical, since both openings establish the very same picnic scene in memory
The second sentence was slower after 'picnic supplies,' since readers had to infer the beer was among them
The second sentence was slower after 'beer,' since immediate repetition produces semantic satiation that delays recognition
explain: When the beer was never mentioned, readers paused to build a bridge — the beer must have been part of the picnic supplies — before the second sentence made sense. That measurable delay is backward inference caught in the act, showing such inferences run online during reading rather than later in memory.
hint: One version states the beer outright; the other makes you connect it.

q: Participants read 'He slipped and dropped the delicate glass pitcher on the wet floor.' On a later surprise recognition round, many confidently accepted a sentence stating the pitcher broke (Johnson, Bransford, & Solomon, 1973). What produced the error?
options: Elaborative inference — readers stored an expected outcome the text never actually stated
Retroactive interference — the recognition sentences overwrote the original ones in memory
Source confusion — readers mixed up which experimenter had spoken which sentence aloud
Anaphoric ambiguity — the pronoun 'it' left unclear which object had hit the floor
explain: Knowing what delicate glassware does when dropped, readers enriched the sentence with its probable consequence and later could not distinguish that addition from the text itself. Comprehension and memory are constructive: what gets stored is the situation the reader built, not a transcript of the words.
hint: The remembered detail was never written — but it was very likely.

q: Singer (1979) found readers did not infer a shovel while reading 'The boy cleared the snow from the stairs,' yet O'Brien et al. (1988) found readers inferred golf from 'his dream of a hole-in-one' before the sport was ever named. How are these findings reconciled?
options: Instrumental inferences can never be drawn online, whereas predictive causal inferences are always mandatory
Spoken presentation blocks elaboration, whereas written presentation encourages it
Elaborative inferences happen online only when the context constrains them strongly enough
Later studies failed to replicate Singer, so his conclusion has been abandoned entirely
explain: A snowy staircase only weakly suggests a shovel, so readers do not bother committing; a hole-in-one dream all but names golf, so they elaborate in advance. Whether elaborative inference runs during reading is not fixed — it scales with how tightly the preceding context points to one conclusion.
hint: Compare how strongly each context points to a single answer.

q: A paragraph about sorting items into piles and not doing too much at once reads as baffling word salad — until people are told it describes doing laundry, whereupon comprehension and later recall jump dramatically (Bransford & Johnson, 1972). What does the hint supply?
options: A mnemonic cue that strengthens rehearsal in the phonological loop during reading
A knowledge framework that lets readers build a coherent situation model of the text
An emotional context that heightens arousal and thereby sharpens memory consolidation afterward
A syntactic template that simplifies the parsing of each individual sentence
explain: The sentences themselves never change — what changes is the reader's ability to anchor them to stored knowledge about laundry. With that schema in place, vague phrases snap into a coherent situation model, and material that was unintelligible becomes both understandable and memorable.
hint: The words stay the same; something outside the text changes.

q: After a stroke, one patient speaks in slow, effortful fragments yet follows conversation well; another produces fluent, melodic streams that carry little meaning and struggles to understand others. Which classical diagnosis pairs with each patient, in order?
options: Wernicke's aphasia, then Broca's aphasia
Conduction aphasia, then global aphasia
Global aphasia, then conduction aphasia
Broca's aphasia, then Wernicke's aphasia
explain: Effortful, telegraphic output with preserved comprehension is the signature of Broca's aphasia, tied to frontal production machinery; fluent but empty speech with poor comprehension marks Wernicke's aphasia, tied to temporal comprehension machinery. This classic double dissociation anchored the earliest brain maps of language.
hint: Match production trouble and comprehension trouble to the right names.

q: Dronkers et al. (2007) re-scanned the preserved brains of Broca's original patients and found damage extending well beyond Broca's area; meanwhile, some patients with lesions confined to Broca's area speak fairly normally. What do modern researchers conclude?
options: Speech production relies on a distributed network rather than one dedicated frontal region
Broca's area is actually dedicated to comprehension, with production housed in the temporal lobe
The original patients were misdiagnosed and never had lasting deficits in producing speech
Production is fully bilateral, so the idea of left-hemisphere dominance should be retired
explain: The founding cases turn out to have had widespread damage, and lesions restricted to Broca's area do not reliably silence speech. Production is now viewed as the work of an interacting network of frontal, temporal, and connecting structures — Broca's area is an important node, not the whole engine.
hint: Neither the lesion data nor the spared cases fit a single-region story.

q: A dense white-matter bundle runs directly between the frontal and temporal language territories. It is nearly absent in most mammals and only weakly developed in non-human primates. What is this tract, and why does it interest researchers studying language evolution?
options: The corpus callosum; it allows the dominant left hemisphere to inhibit the right during speech production
The fornix; it routes linguistic material into hippocampal long-term storage
The arcuate fasciculus; its human elaboration may underpin our unique linguistic capacity
The optic radiation; it delivers written words to the auditory language regions
explain: The arcuate fasciculus wires Broca's and Wernicke's territories into a working circuit. Its striking expansion in humans relative to other primates suggests that fast, direct communication between production and comprehension regions may be part of what makes fully productive language biologically possible.
hint: It is the direct highway between the two classic language regions.

q: Ferré et al. (2012) found that right-hemisphere stroke patients speak a normal number of words but produce noticeably less informative, less coherent speech, and AbdulSabur et al. (2014) saw right temporal activation when people comprehended — but not produced — complex narratives. What role do these data assign the right hemisphere?
options: Controlling articulation whenever the left hemisphere is overloaded by long sentences
Storing the mental lexicon, while the left hemisphere handles all the grammatical work
Processing emotional prosody exclusively, with no contribution to meaning at all
Supporting discourse-level integration, such as global coherence across sentences
explain: Word-level machinery survives right-hemisphere damage — patients still talk fluently — but the big-picture thread frays: their speech wanders and informs less. Combined with imaging showing right temporal engagement during narrative comprehension, this implicates the right hemisphere in stitching sentences into globally coherent discourse.
hint: The deficit shows up across sentences, not within single words.

q: In Beeman et al. (2000), sentences like 'The space shuttle sat waiting for the signal' were flashed to one visual field, then participants named a predictable-but-unstated word such as 'launch.' Naming was fastest after left-visual-field presentation. Why is that informative?
options: Left-field input reaches the left hemisphere first, confirming its dominance in reading
Left-field input goes to the right hemisphere, implicating it in predictive, elaborative inference
Left-field input engages both hemispheres simultaneously, doubling the total processing capacity available
Left-field input bypasses the thalamus, producing a raw speed advantage for any word at all
explain: Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere, so a left-field advantage means the right hemisphere was better primed for the inferred word. That fits a division of labor in which the left hemisphere excels at word-level processing while the right anticipates and elaborates meaning across discourse.
hint: Remember which hemisphere receives each visual field's input.

q: The claim that the particular language you grow up speaking shapes — perhaps even limits — how you perceive and think about the world is known by what name?
options: Universal grammar, associated with Chomsky's nativist program
The poverty of the stimulus, associated with arguments for innateness
Linguistic universalism, the view that all languages express the same core ideas
Linguistic relativity, often called the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
explain: Linguistic relativity — popularized through Sapir and his student Whorf — proposes that a language's categories steer its speakers' cognition and perception. Its opposite, linguistic universalism, treats cross-language differences as surface variation over shared conceptual bedrock; modern evidence supports only modest relativity effects.
hint: Two linguists' names are usually attached to this hypothesis.

q: Whorf's showcase claims — that Inuit contains dozens of words for snow and that Hopi lacks time vocabulary, reshaping perception in each case — later took serious criticism, notably from Pullum (1991). What was the core objection?
options: The effects were real but too small for any behavioral measure to detect them reliably
The linguistic facts themselves were wrong or wildly exaggerated, so the argument had no footing
The claims were only ever tested on bilingual speakers, whose two languages would cancel out each other's effects
Perception of snow and time is fixed at birth, so no vocabulary could possibly alter it
explain: Pullum's famous debunking showed the giant Inuit snow vocabulary is a myth that inflated with each retelling, and the Hopi time claims fared no better under scrutiny. Strong Whorfian conclusions rested on shaky descriptive linguistics, which is why the hypothesis lost favor until subtler evidence revived a weaker version.
hint: Check whether the famous examples were ever accurate descriptions.

q: Russian forces a lexical choice between 'goluboy' (light blue) and 'siniy' (dark blue); English does not. In a color-matching task, which result from Winawer et al. (2007) supports a limited form of linguistic relativity?
options: Russian speakers were faster only when the two blues straddled their category boundary; English speakers showed no such edge
Russian speakers named every shade of blue faster than English speakers across all conditions of the task
English speakers outperformed Russian speakers overall, since a single label simplifies color decisions
Both language groups showed identical cross-category effects, suggesting the light/dark blue boundary is perceptual rather than linguistic in origin
explain: Only Russian speakers gained a cross-category speed advantage — around 10% — and it vanished when both patches fell within one named category, showing the obligatory goluboy/siniy distinction sharpens discrimination right at the linguistic border. That is relativity in a limited sense: language tunes perception locally rather than rebuilding it wholesale.
hint: Look for an effect that appears only where the two names divide.

q: In the pair 'I love cognition. It is my favorite subject,' a transformer-based language model resolves what 'it' refers to without any built-in grammar. Which mechanism does the work?
options: A recurrent memory trace that carries information about each word forward strictly one step at a time
An explicit parse tree constructed from hand-coded syntactic rules
Self-attention scores computed in parallel between every pair of words in the sequence
A lookup table of pronoun-antecedent pairs memorized during training
explain: Self-attention lets the model score how strongly every word relates to every other word simultaneously, so 'it' gets tightly linked to 'cognition' without sequential memory or explicit rules. This parallel relation-scoring is the transformer's core trick and what separates it from earlier recurrent architectures.
hint: The transformer's signature move compares all words at once.

q: Large language models such as GPT-3 are trained on one deceptively simple objective — predict the next word — with no explicit syntax or semantics programmed in, yet they generate fluent, grammatical essays. Why does this bear on the nativist side of the language-acquisition debate?
options: It conclusively proves that human children must also acquire their native languages purely through next-word prediction and nothing else
It shows machines possess an innate universal grammar encoded in their architecture
It demonstrates that grammatical rules are unnecessary for any communication system
It suggests statistical learning from input alone can yield grammar-like ability, weakening claims that innate rules are required
explain: Nativists argued that exposure alone is too impoverished to produce grammar — yet these models reach impressive syntactic competence from raw text statistics. That does not settle how children learn, but it undercuts the claim that grammar cannot in principle emerge from data-driven learning, echoing statistical-learning findings in infants.
hint: Think about what the models were never given, yet still achieved.

q: You want to get from your apartment to a concert across town, but your car will not start and the show begins in an hour. In cognitive psychology, what makes this situation a 'problem'?
options: The stakes are emotionally significant enough to interfere with clear thinking about alternatives
It involves other people whose behavior cannot be predicted
There is a goal, an obstacle in the way, and no immediately obvious route to the solution
It has more than one possible correct answer
explain: A problem, in the cognitive sense, exists whenever a goal is blocked and the solver does not already know the path to it. Emotional stakes, other people, and multiple answers are features some problems have, but the defining structure is an initial state, a goal state, and an obstacle between them (Duncker, 1945; Newell & Simon, 1972).
hint: Think about the minimal structural ingredients every problem shares, big or small.

q: Which of these is the best example of an ill-defined problem?
options: Figuring out how to repair a strained friendship
Solving a Sudoku puzzle
Calculating a 20% tip on a restaurant bill
Finding the shortest checkmate from a given chess position
explain: Repairing a friendship has no single correct answer, no guaranteed procedure, and no clear signal that the goal has been reached — the marks of an ill-defined problem (Reitman, 1964; Kitchener, 1983). Sudoku, tip arithmetic, and chess positions all have clearly specified states and procedures that lead to a verifiable answer.
hint: Ask which situation lacks a clear finish line and a guaranteed procedure.

q: In Newell and Simon's (1972) problem space theory, what is an 'operator'?
options: The person or system doing the solving
An action that transforms one problem state into another
The mental representation of the goal state
A stored memory trace of a similar problem solved successfully in the past
explain: Problem space theory treats solving as a search from an initial state to a goal state through intermediate states, and operators are the permitted moves that carry the solver from one state to the next. Legal moves in chess or individual pouring steps in a measuring task are operators.
hint: In a board game, this would be a legal move, not a player or a position.

q: After weeks of your houseplants dying, you finally admit something is wrong, research watering and light needs, adjust their care, and then watch over the next month to see whether the new leaves stay healthy. That final month of watching corresponds to which part of the problem-solving cycle?
options: Representing the problem mentally
Allocating mental and physical resources for working on the problem
Generating candidate solution strategies
Evaluating whether the chosen solution actually worked
explain: Problem solving does not end when action is taken — the cycle closes with monitoring progress and verifying the solution's effectiveness (Pretz et al., 2003; D'Zurilla & Goldfried, 1971). Watching the plants after changing their care is exactly that verification step.
hint: One step of the cycle can only happen after a solution has been put into action.

q: A software team builds a program that plays chess flawlessly, and another that helps users decide which city to relocate to. Why is the second task so much harder to automate?
options: Relocation decisions require more raw computing power than chess does
Human emotions cannot be represented in any formal system
The initial state, goal state, and available moves of a relocation decision are not clearly specifiable, so no step-by-step procedure can guarantee a solution
Relocation problems have too many intermediate states for a computer to search
explain: Chess is well-defined: every state and legal move can be written down, so algorithms can grind toward a verifiable answer. Choosing where to live is ill-defined — the goal itself is fuzzy, many answers could count as correct, and nothing confirms you got it right (Reitman, 1964). That structure, not raw computing power, is what resists automation.
hint: Compare how precisely each problem's states and moves can be written down.

q: A researcher writes a computer simulation intended to model how people solve letter-arithmetic puzzles. The program solves every puzzle instantly and never makes an error. As a model of human cognition, this result is
options: a failure, because a good simulation should reproduce human steps and missteps, not outperform them
a success, because faster performance shows the underlying algorithm is correct
a success, because the program reached the same answers people eventually reach
a failure, because computer simulations are incapable of revealing anything about internal mental processes
explain: When simulations are used to study cognition, the goal is to mimic the human process — including errors, delays, and distraction by unimportant details (Simon & Newell, 1962). A program that vastly outperforms people may be impressive engineering, but it cannot reveal the mechanisms people actually use.
hint: Ask what the simulation is supposed to imitate: the answer, or the human route to it.

q: Edward Thorndike (1911) placed cats in puzzle boxes and timed their escapes across repeated attempts. Which view of problem solving did his findings support?
options: Problems are solved when the solver suddenly restructures how the whole situation is mentally represented
Problems are solved reproductively, by trial and error strengthened through experience
Problems are solved by working backwards from the goal state
Problems are solved by breaking goals into a series of subgoals
explain: Thorndike's cats escaped a little faster with each attempt, which he explained with the Law of Effect: responses followed by satisfying outcomes are strengthened while unsatisfying ones fade. That gradual, experience-driven improvement is the signature of reproductive, trial-and-error problem solving.
hint: The cats' escape times improved gradually, not in one sudden leap.

q: Maria has been staring at a geometry puzzle, treating a certain line as a triangle's base. When she suddenly re-pictures that same line as the diameter of a circle, the answer becomes obvious. Which Gestalt concept best captures what just happened?
options: Reproductive thinking drawing on a remembered rule
The Law of Effect strengthening a successful response
Means-end analysis reducing the distance to the goal
Restructuring — changing the mental representation of the problem
explain: Gestalt psychologists argued that productive problem solving hinges on restructuring: actively re-representing a problem's elements until a new organization reveals the solution (Wertheimer, 1959). Maria's shift from 'base of a triangle' to 'diameter of a circle' is precisely that representational flip, which is why the answer arrived all at once.
hint: Nothing on the page changed — only how she organized it in her mind.

q: An experienced plumber diagnoses a leak by combining the drip pattern she sees under the sink with her memory of hundreds of similar repairs. In information-processing terms, she is integrating
options: bottom-up information from the environment with top-down knowledge from past experience
divergent thinking with convergent thinking
reproductive thinking with the Law of Effect
proximal sensory cues drawn from the goal state with distal semantic cues drawn from the initial state
explain: Understanding a problem means pooling two streams: perceptual data available in the current situation (bottom-up) and stored knowledge, strategies, and beliefs from prior experience (top-down) (Kotovsky et al., 1985; Newell & Simon, 1972). The drip pattern is the first stream; her repair history is the second.
hint: One stream comes in through her eyes right now; the other was stored years ago.

q: You finally fix your bike's slipping chain, only to discover the repositioned wheel now rubs the brake pad — sending you back to the toolbox armed with what the first repair taught you. This pattern illustrates which property of problem solving?
options: Functional fixedness
The feeling-of-warmth gradient
Its cyclical, recursive nature — solutions surface new problems, and steps repeat as needed
The categorical distinction between well-defined problems and ill-defined problems with unclear goals
explain: Problem solving rarely ends cleanly: reaching one solution often reveals a new or related problem, and the solver re-enters the cycle carrying forward what the last round taught (Hayes, 1989; Sternberg, 1986). The chain fix creating a brake problem — and informing the next repair — is that recursion in action.
hint: Solving the first issue both created the next one and equipped you for it.

q: Suppose problem solving in animals worked purely by sudden insight rather than incremental learning. In Thorndike's puzzle-box studies, what should the cats' escape-time curves have looked like?
options: A smooth, gradual decline in escape time across trials
Little improvement for many trials, then an abrupt drop to fast escapes once the mechanism was grasped
Immediate fast escapes from the very first trial onward
Random escape times with no relationship to trial number
explain: Insight predicts an all-at-once grasp of the solution: long floundering, then a sudden and lasting drop in escape time. Thorndike instead observed smooth, gradual improvement across trials, which is why he concluded that learning was incremental trial and error rather than sudden restructuring.
hint: Sketch the curve each theory predicts before comparing them to what Thorndike saw.

q: Gestalt psychologists argued that trial-and-error accounts of problem solving were incomplete. Which everyday experience gives their critique the most direct support?
options: Practicing free throws every afternoon makes you a steadily more accurate shooter over several weeks of training
A child learns to avoid a hot stove after touching it once
You solve long-division problems faster after doing many of them
A riddle you abandoned suddenly resolves itself, complete and certain, while you are doing something else
explain: Gradual skill gains fit a reproductive, practice-strengthened account. What that account cannot explain is a solution arriving fully formed with no incremental progress — the a-ha experience. Sudden restructuring of the problem's representation, not accumulated trial and error, is the Gestalt explanation for such moments (Wertheimer, 1959).
hint: Three of these show gradual strengthening; one shows something arriving all at once.

q: You need to prop a door open on a windy day. A heavy hardcover book sits on the shelf beside you, yet you wander the house searching for a doorstop. Which barrier to problem solving is at work?
options: Mental set
Irrelevant information
Functional fixedness
Means-end analysis
explain: Functional fixedness is the tendency to see an object only in terms of its customary function — a book is for reading, so its potential as a heavy weight goes unnoticed (Duncker, 1945). The barrier concerns object use, which distinguishes it from mental set, a rut in solution procedures.
hint: The obstacle here is how you categorize an object, not which procedure you repeat.

q: In Maier's (1931) two-string task, people must tie together two hanging strings that cannot be reached at the same time. Solvers succeed by tying a hammer to one string and swinging it like a pendulum. Why does placing the hammer inside a toolbox make the task even harder?
options: The toolbox context cements the hammer's identity as a tool, deepening fixedness on its usual function
The toolbox physically hides the hammer so participants never notice it
Opening and searching the toolbox consumes attention and working-memory capacity that the solution itself requires
The toolbox suggests the solution involves building something
explain: Solving the task requires re-seeing the hammer as a swinging weight. Encountering it nestled among other tools strengthens the 'hammer = tool' categorization, making the leap to 'pendulum weight' even less likely. Context can deepen functional fixedness rather than merely fail to help.
hint: Think about what the surrounding context does to the hammer's perceived category.

q: Duncker's candle task asks people to mount a candle on a wall using matches, tacks, and a box. What change made participants roughly twice as likely to solve it, and why?
options: Giving them substantially more time to work, because the solution requires an exhaustive search of combinations
Presenting the box empty, because it was no longer perceived purely as a container
Providing a larger box, because the candle fit on it more securely
Demonstrating the tacks first, because tacks are the least familiar object
explain: When the box arrives filled with matches, its role as a container dominates and its potential as a candle shelf goes unseen. Emptying it loosens that functional interpretation, and solution rates roughly doubled (Duncker, 1945) — evidence that fixedness depends partly on how objects are presented, not just on the solver.
hint: The successful change altered how one object's function was perceived, not how hard the mechanics were.

q: Luchins (1942) had people solve a series of water-jar measuring puzzles that all yielded to the same three-jar formula, then gave them puzzles with a far simpler shortcut. What did the experienced group do, and what does it show?
options: They discovered the shortcut even faster than newcomers did, showing that practice on a problem type transfers broadly
They refused to continue, showing motivation collapses when routines fail
They alternated randomly between methods, showing procedures never stabilize
They kept applying the old formula, showing a mental set can blind solvers to simpler methods
explain: Participants trained on the B − A − 2C pattern kept using it on later puzzles solvable in one or two steps, while a control group given those puzzles first found the simple routes almost every time (Luchins, 1942). A practiced procedure had become a mental set — a rut of past success that hid better options.
hint: Compare the trained group with a control group that met the later puzzles cold.

q: A riddle opens with 'Suppose you are driving the bus,' then lists passenger counts at every stop before asking for the driver's name. Most people, busy tracking the arithmetic, miss that the answer is their own name. Which barrier does this illustrate?
options: Functional fixedness
Failure to ignore irrelevant information
An overly narrow problem space
Unnecessary constraints imposed on the solution
explain: The passenger arithmetic is a decoy: none of it bears on the question asked. People who dive into the numbers are led down a dead end by irrelevant details — a barrier skilled solvers overcome by first deciding which information actually matters (Halpern, 2013).
hint: Ask which details in the riddle actually bear on the question being asked.

q: People trying the nine-dot puzzle almost always assume their four lines must stay inside the square the dots imply. If an experimenter simply tells them lines may extend beyond the dots, what happens?
options: Nearly everyone then solves the puzzle immediately, confirming the self-imposed boundary was the only real barrier
Performance gets worse, because the extra instruction adds cognitive load
Solution rates barely improve unless the hint is paired with cues that give away part of the answer
Only participants high in ideational fluency benefit from the hint
explain: Removing the self-imposed boundary assumption turns out to be insufficient: told they could draw outside the square, participants still mostly failed unless additional partial-solution cues were provided (Burnham & Davis, 1969; Weisberg & Alba, 1981). Unnecessary constraints matter, but dropping one does not by itself deliver the answer.
hint: The obvious explanation for the puzzle's difficulty was directly put to the experiment — and came up short.

q: While brainstorming names for a new coffee shop, Priya lists forty possibilities in ten minutes, from puns to invented words. Which mode of thought is she exercising?
options: Divergent thinking
Convergent thinking
Reproductive thinking
Means-end analysis
explain: Divergent thinking generates many candidate solutions fanning out from a single starting point, and Guilford (1967) identified it as the core of creativity. Convergent thinking does the opposite — narrowing the options toward one conventional answer.
hint: Is her thinking fanning outward toward many options, or narrowing toward one?

q: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) asked solvers to rate their 'feeling of warmth' every 15 seconds while working. How did the ratings differ between algebra problems and insight puzzles?
options: Warmth rose steadily for both, but faster for insight puzzles
Warmth stayed flat for both until the moment of solution
Warmth predicted final success on insight puzzles but not on algebra problems
Warmth climbed steadily toward solution on algebra problems, but solvers of insight puzzles could not sense how close they were
explain: On step-by-step algebra, people tracked their own progress with fair accuracy, warming gradually as the answer approached. On insight puzzles, warmth ratings were poor predictors — solutions arrived without warning. Metcalfe and Wiebe took this as evidence for two distinct kinds of problems served by different cognitive processes.
hint: One kind of problem lets you feel yourself approaching the answer; the other does not.

q: In Maier's two-string study, the experimenter 'accidentally' brushed a string, setting it swinging; many stuck participants solved the task soon after — yet almost none credited the swinging string when asked how they got the answer. What does this suggest about insight?
options: Participants recognized the hint perfectly well but deliberately concealed the help they had received from it
The restructuring behind insight can be triggered and unfold outside conscious awareness
Hints only work when solvers consciously register and apply them
The swinging string was a coincidence unrelated to the solutions
explain: The cue clearly worked — solutions clustered right after it — but solvers could not report it, and they cited useless cues just as often as the useful one. Maier (1931) concluded that the reorganization producing insight happens beneath awareness, which is why a-ha moments feel like they come from nowhere.
hint: Solutions followed the cue reliably, but people's reports of the cue did not.

q: A researcher wants a quick, countable measure of creative capacity. Following Guilford (1956), she asks volunteers to list every use they can imagine for a brick, then tallies the usable ideas. What is this measure called?
options: Convergent validity
Feeling of warmth
Ideational fluency
Practical intelligence
explain: Ideational fluency quantifies creativity as the number of relevant ideas a person can produce for a given prompt — uses for a brick or a pencil, taglines for a product, arrangements of a room (Guilford, 1956; Bereiter, 1960). Producing more usable ideas is taken to indicate a more creative thinker.
hint: The measure literally counts how many ideas flow from a single prompt.

q: In Sternberg's (1985) triarchic theory, a chef who invents an original dessert by combining techniques she already commands to meet a novel ingredient list is chiefly displaying
options: creative intelligence — using existing knowledge to handle novelty with appropriate, valuable ideas
analytical intelligence — the academic puzzle-and-analogy solving skill that standard IQ measurements capture
practical intelligence — street-smart handling of everyday situations
ideational fluency — the sheer number of dessert ideas she can list
explain: The triarchic theory splits intelligence into analytical (academic puzzle-solving), practical (everyday street smarts), and creative facets. Deploying an existing skill base to produce something novel, situation-appropriate, and valuable is the creative facet by definition — exactly what invention around a new ingredient list demands.
hint: Match the scenario to the facet defined by novelty plus appropriateness, not by volume of ideas.

q: If creativity and problem-solving ability are genuinely linked, what should happen when people complete both a creativity inventory and a problem-solving inventory — and what did Zirhlioglu (2012) actually find?
options: Scores should be unrelated, and they were — the two abilities are independent
Creativity should predict only artistic tasks, and that is what the data showed
High creativity should impair systematic solving, and scores correlated negatively
Scores should rise together, and a positive relationship is what emerged
explain: Zirhlioglu (2012) administered Heppner and Petersen's problem-solving inventory alongside Raudsepp's creativity scale and found the two moved in the same direction: more creative respondents reported stronger problem solving. That positive association fits the view that generating many novel options aids solution finding.
hint: Recall which direction the association ran when both scales were given together.

q: Chase and Simon (1973) showed chess masters and beginners a board for five seconds and asked them to reconstruct it. When the pieces came from real games, masters excelled. What happened when the pieces were scattered at random?
options: The masters' advantage grew, since they could impose structure on the chaos
Masters performed no better than beginners
Masters recalled fewer pieces than beginners did
Both groups improved because random boards carry less information
explain: The masters' recall edge came from matching real positions to thousands of stored game patterns and remembering them as chunks. Random boards match no stored patterns, so the chunking advantage evaporated and masters dropped to beginner levels — expertise is organized domain knowledge, not superior general memory.
hint: The masters' edge depended on the arrangement matching something already stored.

q: Asked to sort physics problems into groups, beginners cluster them by surface features — 'these all mention springs' — while experts group them differently. On what basis do experts categorize, according to Chi et al. (1981)?
options: By how long each problem takes to read and understand
By the mathematical difficulty of the calculations each problem's solution would ultimately require
By the underlying principles the problems share with previously solved ones
By the physical objects that appear in each problem's story
explain: Experts see past a problem's cover story to the principle that governs its solution, grouping a spring problem with a pendulum problem when both turn on the same underlying idea. This principle-based categorization lets them match new problems to solution plans they already own (Chi et al., 1981).
hint: Experts look beneath the story a problem happens to be dressed in.

q: Watching an expert and a novice begin the same unfamiliar-looking repair, you notice the expert spends noticeably longer just studying the situation before touching a tool. Why does this early slowness pay off?
options: Careful analysis lets experts pick a principled plan they then execute rapidly and largely automatically
It signals conscientiousness, which correlates with successful outcomes
Experts need extra time because their larger knowledge base is slower to search
Delaying physical action reduces the emotional arousal that would otherwise impair fine motor control during the repair
explain: Experts front-load the work: they analyze and organize the problem, match it to principles from past cases, and only then act — after which execution runs on largely automatic processing (Chi et al., 1981; Lesgold, 1988). Novices start faster but burn time in trial and error, so the slow starters finish ahead.
hint: Contrast where each solver spends time: before acting versus during repeated attempts.

q: A veteran engineer and a first-year hire both face a design problem whose best solution violates standard practice in their field. Who is more likely to find it, and why?
options: The veteran, because deeper expertise reliably improves solution quality across all problem types
The veteran, because automatic processing conserves capacity that can be redirected toward generating novel ideas
The first-year hire, because novices have superior working memory capacity
The first-year hire, because no entrenched mental set steers them toward conventional approaches
explain: Deep experience builds strong mental sets and automatic responses; those usually help, but when a problem demands abandoning standard practice they steer experts down familiar roads. Lacking those ruts, a newcomer can be freer to consider unconventional options — the situation where expertise becomes a liability.
hint: This particular problem punishes exactly what years of expertise build up.

q: Planning a cross-country move, Dev keeps the end goal in view while setting a chain of subgoals — book movers by May, sell the car by June, secure housing by July — each chosen to shrink the gap between where he is and where he wants to end up. Which strategy is he using?
options: Working backwards from the goal state
Means-end analysis
An exhaustive algorithm
Reproductive trial and error
explain: Means-end analysis keeps the final goal in mind while selecting subgoals that each reduce the distance between the current state and the goal state, with room to adjust at every step (Newell & Simon, 1972). It differs from working backwards, which starts at the end point and reasons in reverse order.
hint: The giveaway is the chain of difference-reducing subgoals, not reverse-order reasoning.

q: A computer beats any human at the Tower of Hanoi, yet the information-processing approach still treats human and machine solvers as usefully comparable. What is the key processing difference behind the performance gap?
options: Computers use heuristics while humans rely on exhaustive algorithms
Humans cannot represent the problem's changing states at all
Computers can evaluate all possible moves at once, while limited working memory lets humans hold only a few candidate steps
Machines lack executive control processes, so nothing slows down their search
explain: Both humans and machines combine incoming information with stored memory under a limited-capacity central processor, which is why the comparison is fruitful. The gap is capacity: a computer can churn through every legal move, while human working memory holds only a handful of possibilities at a time — forcing people onto heuristics where machines run exhaustive algorithms.
hint: Both are processors of information — compare how many possibilities each can juggle at once.

q: You can't find your wallet, so you think back to where you last used it and work out where it must be now. This process of drawing new conclusions from information you already have is called what?
options: Reasoning
Perceptual organization
Memory consolidation
Selective attention
explain: Reasoning extrapolates from what you already believe or remember to reach conclusions you never directly observed — here, inferring the wallet's location from memory. Perception and attention handle incoming information; consolidation stabilizes memory traces after the fact.
hint: Think of the stage of cognition that goes beyond the information you already possess.

q: Which statement best captures the core difference between deduction and induction?
options: Induction guarantees a true conclusion, while deduction can only ever make a conclusion more likely
Deduction always moves from single, concrete observations up to broad laws, while induction applies broad laws back down to single cases
Deduction concerns facts about the physical world, while induction concerns beliefs about mental states
Deduction yields certain conclusions when its premises are true; induction yields conclusions that are probable at best
explain: The signature of deduction is certainty: with true premises and a valid form, the conclusion must be true. Induction extrapolates beyond observed cases, so even its strongest conclusions stay probabilistic — the next observation could always break the pattern.
hint: One process offers a guarantee; the other offers only a strong bet.

q: Consider this argument: 'All metals are magnetic. Copper is a metal. Therefore, copper is magnetic.' Copper is not, in fact, magnetic. What is the correct verdict on the argument?
options: It is invalid, because a genuinely valid argument can never lead from its premises to a conclusion that is false in the real world
It is valid: the conclusion follows from the premises, but the false first premise makes the conclusion untrue
It is invalid because it commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent
It is both valid and true, since validity is what defines truth within a logical system
explain: Validity is a property of an argument's structure: given those premises, the conclusion follows necessarily. Truth is a separate question about the premises themselves. Because 'all metals are magnetic' is false, this argument is valid yet unsound, and its conclusion fails.
hint: Separate the form of the argument from the accuracy of its premises.

q: Theo is certain he left his umbrella by the door, but it isn't there. First he concludes that one of his assumptions must be wrong; then he starts checking the spots where he has misplaced it before. Which reasoning processes are at work, in order?
options: Induction first (guessing likely spots from experience), then deduction (confirming the guess with logical certainty)
Deduction throughout, since each step follows with certainty from what he knows
Deduction first (a premise must be false), then induction (generalizing from past misplacements)
Induction throughout, since nothing about misplaced objects is ever certain
explain: Concluding that some premise must be false when a logically required prediction fails is deductive: if the umbrella isn't where the premises entail it must be, a premise is wrong. Searching past misplacement spots is inductive — projecting previous cases onto a probable current location.
hint: One step follows with certainty from premises; the other generalizes from history.

q: Formal logic establishes that only 24 of the 256 possible categorical syllogism forms are valid, yet people routinely endorse invalid ones. What does this mismatch imply about the relationship between logic and the psychology of reasoning?
options: Logic provides a normative benchmark against which actual human inference can be measured, much as the physical world serves as a benchmark for perception
Logic is a descriptive theory of thought, so the mismatch means the logical rules themselves must be revised
The mismatch shows that human reasoning is essentially random and cannot be studied systematically
People who endorse invalid forms lack the capacity for deductive thought altogether
explain: Logic is normative, not descriptive: it specifies which inferences are guaranteed to preserve truth, regardless of how people actually think. Psychologists then compare real performance against that standard, just as perception researchers compare experience against the physical stimulus.
hint: Ask whether logic describes minds or sets a standard for them.

q: A gardener reasons: 'If the sprinklers ran overnight, the lawn is wet this morning. The sprinklers ran overnight. So the lawn is wet.' Which deductive form is this?
options: Modus tollens
Denying the antecedent
Affirming the consequent
Modus ponens
explain: Affirming the antecedent — modus ponens — observes that the 'if' condition holds and validly concludes the 'then' part, essentially restating the conditional. Evans and colleagues (1993) found people are nearly flawless on this form, unlike its trickier valid cousin that denies the consequent.
hint: Notice which half of the conditional rule gets observed to be true.

q: 'If the power stayed on all night, the freezer will still be frozen solid. The freezer has thawed. Therefore, the power went out.' What kind of inference is this, and is it valid?
options: Modus tollens — valid: denying the consequent licenses denying the antecedent
Modus ponens — valid: observing the antecedent licenses affirming the consequent
Affirming the consequent — invalid: a thawed freezer could have several other causes
Denying the antecedent — invalid: the power could fail without the freezer thawing
explain: This is modus tollens: the rule promises a frozen freezer whenever power persists, the promised consequence failed to appear, so the antecedent must have failed too. The form is fully valid, though people endorse it far less reliably than modus ponens.
hint: Work backward from an expected consequence that failed to appear.

q: 'If Priya went for a run, her sneakers will be by the door. Her sneakers are by the door — so she must have gone for a run.' Why do logicians reject this inference?
options: It denies the antecedent, a form that never yields a valid conclusion
The conclusion happens to be false in this instance, and no argument with a false conclusion can possibly be valid
It affirms the consequent: sneakers by the door could arise for reasons the rule never excludes
Its premises contradict one another, so no conclusion can follow from them
explain: The conditional only promises sneakers if Priya ran; it says nothing about what else might put sneakers by the door. Inferring the antecedent from an observed consequent is affirming the consequent, an invalid form — she may simply store them there every day.
hint: The rule runs in one direction; check whether the inference runs the other way.

q: Evans and Curtis-Holmes (2005) had people judge syllogisms whose conclusions were believable or unbelievable, either at their own pace or within a few seconds. Based on dual-process accounts of reasoning, what should the strict deadline do?
options: Eliminate belief bias entirely, because a short deadline leaves no time to retrieve prior beliefs about the conclusion
Amplify belief bias, since haste forces reliance on fast believability judgments over slow analysis
Leave accuracy unchanged, since logical validity is computed automatically
Improve overall accuracy, because intuition is better calibrated than deliberation
explain: Dual-process accounts treat belief bias as the fast, intuitive system substituting believability for validity. A deadline blocks the slow, analytic system that could override it, so rushed participants leaned even harder on whether conclusions merely sounded true.
hint: Consider which of the two reasoning systems a deadline switches off.

q: Wason (1968) showed people cards E, K, 4, and 7 (each with a letter on one side, a number on the other) plus the rule 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.' Besides E, which card must be flipped, and why?
options: The 4, because finding a vowel on its reverse would confirm the rule holds
The K, because the rule concerns the relationship between letters and numbers
Both the 4 and the 7, because every number card bears on a rule about numbers
The 7, because finding a vowel on its reverse would prove the rule false
explain: A rule is tested by hunting for potential falsifiers. An odd-numbered card could hide a vowel — the one pairing the rule forbids. The even card can prove nothing: a consonant behind it is perfectly compatible with the rule, so flipping it reflects confirmation-seeking, not testing.
hint: Ask which cards could possibly prove the rule false, not which could agree with it.

q: Griggs and Cox (1982) recast Wason's card problem as an officer checking for underage drinking in a bar, and the solution rate leapt from about 4% to 73%. What does this content effect suggest?
options: People apply the abstract rules of formal logic far more accurately whenever getting the answer wrong carries higher real-world stakes
Reasoning improves when a rule maps onto familiar, concrete situations, even though the logical structure is unchanged
The drinking version is logically simpler because fewer cards genuinely bear on the rule
Later participants were simply more practiced with logic problems than Wason's original participants
explain: The two versions share an identical logical skeleton; only the content changed. Performance soared because a familiar social rule lets people match the situation to well-practiced real-life patterns — spotting rule-breakers — instead of analyzing abstract letter-number forms.
hint: Compare the logical structure of the two versions before crediting anything else.

q: Johnson-Laird's mental model theory holds that people evaluate syllogisms by imagining the situations described rather than by applying syntactic rules. Which pattern of results best fits this account?
options: People judge arguments about abstract A's and B's just as accurately as arguments about dogs and beards
Validity judgments are unaffected by how easy the premise content is to visualize
People reason better with concrete, picturable content, which supports building and inspecting a simulation of the premises
Validity judgments track nothing except whether qualifying words such as 'some' and 'all' in the conclusion match those appearing in the premises
explain: Mental model theory says reasoners simulate the described situation — picturing bins, price tags, people — and then inspect that simulation for counterexamples. This predicts an advantage for easily visualized content, something a purely syntactic rule-applier would not care about.
hint: The theory claims we simulate scenes rather than manipulate symbols.

q: Every espresso you've bought at your corner café has been excellent, so you conclude tomorrow's will be too. What is the defining feature of this kind of inference?
options: It extends past observations beyond the data, so its conclusion is probable rather than guaranteed
Its conclusion follows with complete certainty, provided all of the underlying premises happen to be true
It moves from a general rule to a conclusion about one specific case
It requires consciously computing the exact probability of each outcome
explain: Inductive inference projects past regularities onto unobserved cases. However many excellent espressos accumulate, tomorrow's cup is not guaranteed — this is Hume's point that inductive conclusions are probable extrapolations, never certainties, no matter how reliable they feel.
hint: Could the conclusion still be wrong even if every observation is accurate?

q: 'Nearly everyone in my building owns a bike, so my new neighbor Ana probably owns one too.' Which type of inductive inference is this?
options: Generalization, since it extends observations of a limited sample outward to an entire population
Argument from analogy, since Ana resembles the building's other residents
Bayesian inference, since a prior belief about Ana is updated with new evidence
Statistical syllogism, since it moves from a group-level pattern to one individual
explain: A statistical syllogism runs from a statistic about a group to a conclusion about one member: most residents own bikes, so this particular resident probably does. Generalization travels the opposite direction — from observed cases outward to the whole category.
hint: Note the direction of travel: from a group-level statistic toward one person.

q: Two food writers each conclude that a city's food scene is superb. One ate at 40 restaurants across many neighborhoods and cuisines; the other ate at three restaurants on the same block. Why is the first conclusion stronger?
options: Because the first writer's conclusion is deductively valid rather than inductive
Because larger, more varied samples support stronger generalizations to the whole category
Because visiting enough restaurants converts an induction into a logical certainty
Because the strength of an inductive argument depends mainly on how confident the reasoner feels
explain: Inductive strength grows with sample size and with the sample's diversity relative to the category's variability. Forty restaurants spanning neighborhoods and cuisines represent a city's whole food scene far better than three doors on a single block ever could — though certainty is never reached.
hint: What makes a sample earn the right to speak for the whole category?

q: A toddler hears the word 'zebra' once, applied to one animal, yet immediately uses it for other zebras — and never for the fence behind them. On a Bayesian view of induction, what makes this one-shot leap possible?
options: Children are born already knowing the names of most natural categories
Toddlers avoid induction altogether, waiting for deductive proof of a word's meaning before using it
Prior expectations — such as that whole objects usually receive names — constrain which generalizations the single example supports
One example is logically sufficient to fix a word's meaning without any further assumptions
explain: Bayesian inference combines a prior — expectations held before the data arrive, like 'labels usually name whole objects and their categories' — with the new example. The prior collapses the space of possible meanings, letting one instance license a sweeping yet accurate generalization.
hint: One data point cannot do it alone; what narrows the possibilities beforehand?

q: In Ross, Lepper, and Hubbard (1975), people received fake feedback saying they were excellent (or terrible) at spotting genuine suicide notes. Even after being told the feedback was invented, their self-ratings still tracked the fake scores. Which tendency does this illustrate?
options: Anchoring: the first number they were given served as a reference point that dragged all later self-estimates toward it
Confirmation bias: once a belief forms, people favor evidence that supports it and discount evidence that undermines it
The affect heuristic: the emotional sting of the feedback distorted their probability estimates
The framing effect: describing identical scores positively or negatively changed their self-ratings
explain: Once participants formed a belief about their skill, they discounted the disconfirming revelation that the scores were fabricated. That asymmetry — clutching supportive evidence while shrugging off contrary evidence — is confirmation bias, first named by Wason (1960).
hint: The telling detail is what happened after the debriefing.

q: After a week of wall-to-wall news coverage of a plane crash, Marco cancels his flight and drives instead, though driving is statistically riskier. Which shortcut best explains his risk judgment?
options: The availability heuristic — vivid, recent examples spring to mind and inflate the event's perceived frequency
Anchoring — the crash's widely reported death toll anchored his estimate of driving's safety
The representativeness heuristic — the crash closely matches his mental prototype of what a transportation disaster looks like
The status quo bias — he simply reverted to the mode of travel he has always known best
explain: The availability heuristic substitutes ease of retrieval for actual frequency: saturation coverage makes crashes leap to mind, so flying feels dangerous. Lichtenstein and colleagues (1978) found the same mechanism inflating estimates for memorable causes of death like tornadoes.
hint: Ask what just became extremely easy to call to mind, and why.

q: People rate shark attacks as a far bigger threat than drowning, though drowning kills vastly more swimmers each year. Slovic and colleagues traced such misjudgments to the sense of dread an outcome evokes. Which mechanism is at work?
options: The anchoring heuristic: the first shark-attack statistics people encounter anchor all of their later risk judgments
The conjunction fallacy: sharks and death are judged as a compound event
A statistical syllogism: reasoning from the group of all swimmers to one swimmer
The affect heuristic: the strength of the emotional reaction serves as an index of how likely the event is
explain: The affect heuristic converts the intensity of an emotional response into a frequency estimate: dread-soaked outcomes feel common. Sharks trigger vivid dread while quiet drowning does not, so the far rarer threat gets rated as the larger one.
hint: The judgment tracks a feeling's intensity rather than any statistic.

q: Tversky and Kahneman (1974) spun a rigged wheel that stopped at either 10 or 65, then asked people to estimate the percentage of United Nations countries that are African. What happened, and why?
options: Estimates were unaffected, since everyone recognized the wheel as irrelevant to geography
Participants who saw 65 gave far higher estimates — the arbitrary starting number anchored their judgment
Participants who saw 10 gave higher estimates, overcorrecting away from the low anchor
Estimates clustered tightly around the true value because individual errors simply averaged out across the whole group
explain: An obviously arbitrary number still served as an anchor: judgments start from the initial figure and adjust insufficiently, even when that starting point carries zero information. Ariely and colleagues (2003) later showed the same effect using digits of people's social security numbers.
hint: Consider what a starting number does to later adjustment, relevant or not.

q: Tom is quiet, loves poetry, and wears wire-rimmed glasses. Asked whether Tom is more likely a literature scholar or a truck driver, most people say scholar — even though truck drivers vastly outnumber literature scholars. Which shortcut drives this?
options: The availability heuristic
The anchoring heuristic
The representativeness heuristic
The affect heuristic
