explain: Judging Tom by how well he resembles the stereotype of a category — rather than by how many people each category actually contains — is the representativeness heuristic. The resemblance is real, but it swamps the base rates that should dominate the judgment.
hint: The judgment leans on resemblance to a mental picture of the category.

q: Given a sketch of 'Linda' as a socially engaged philosophy major, 85% of Tversky and Kahneman's (1983) respondents ranked 'bank teller and active feminist' as more probable than 'bank teller.' Why is that ranking logically impossible?
options: Because feminist activists are rarely employed as bank tellers in real life
Because the probability of a compound statement can never legitimately be compared with that of a simple one
Because the description of Linda was deliberately written to be uninformative about her career
Because everyone who fits the compound description is also a bank teller, so the conjunction can never be the likelier of the two
explain: Set logic forbids the ranking: feminist bank tellers form a subset of bank tellers, so the compound can be at most equally probable, never more. Representativeness overrides this — the feminist detail fits Linda's sketch so well that fit masquerades as probability. This is the conjunction fallacy.
hint: Draw the two groups as circles and check which one contains the other.

q: A witness says a hit-and-run cab was blue. Blue cabs make up 15% of the city's fleet, and the witness identifies colors correctly 80% of the time under matching conditions. Most people put the odds the cab was blue near 80%; the true answer is 41%. What are they neglecting?
options: The base rate: green cabs are so common that many 'blue' reports are actually misidentified green cabs
The witness's accuracy: 80% reliability is far too low to count as usable evidence
The conjunction rule: 'blue and misidentified' must be less likely than 'blue' alone
The framing of the question: stating the numbers as percentages rather than natural frequencies misleads them
explain: With only 15% of cabs blue, the pool of green cabs is so large that even a 20% error rate produces many false 'blue' sightings — enough to rival the true ones. Trusting the evidence while ignoring the underlying proportion is base-rate neglect, the Bayesian prior left out of the math.
hint: Imagine the witness viewing all one hundred cabs and tally the mistaken reports.

q: Levin and Gaeth (1988) labeled physically identical ground beef either '75% lean' or '25% fat.' What did they find when shoppers actually tasted it?
options: The labels shifted what shoppers said they would be willing to pay beforehand but left their actual taste ratings untouched
The beef labeled '25% fat' was rated tastier, since fat is what carries flavor
The beef labeled '75% lean' was rated as tasting better — the frame reached into the eating experience itself
Ratings were identical, because direct tasting overrides anything printed on a label
explain: Framing didn't stop at the moment of choice: the same beef described by its lean percentage was reported as genuinely tasting better than beef described by its fat percentage. Positive frames shape not just decisions but the downstream sensory experience of what was chosen.
hint: The surprise is what the label did after the purchase decision was over.

q: Expected utility theory, rooted in Bernoulli's 18th-century work, treats choosers as rational value-maximizers. Faced with several options, what does it predict a person will do?
options: Choose whichever option preserves their current situation with the least disruption
Choose the option with the highest expected value, weighing each outcome by its probability
Choose the option that minimizes the worst conceivable loss, regardless of how large the potential gains might be
Choose whichever option springs to mind most quickly and feels most familiar
explain: Expected utility theory models choosers as maximizers: multiply each outcome's value by its probability and pick the option with the highest total. Kahneman and Tversky's research program succeeded precisely by cataloguing the systematic ways real choices depart from this baseline.
hint: The theory treats every chooser as a careful calculating economist.

q: In the Ultimatum Game (Guth et al., 1982), a proposer offers a split of $10 and the responder can accept or reject it — rejection leaves both with nothing. Responders routinely reject offers around $2. Why does this trouble expected utility theory?
options: It doesn't: rejecting lowball offers builds a reputation for toughness that pays off across future rounds of the game
Because rational proposers should have offered exactly half of the pot
Two dollars beats nothing, so refusing sacrifices real value just to punish unfairness — a choice pure value-maximization cannot predict
Because the game involves two people, and utility theory covers only individual choices
explain: Any positive offer beats zero, so a strict value-maximizer accepts $2. Rejection sacrifices real money to punish a raw deal, showing that outrage and fairness concerns enter the calculation — a systematic violation of expected utility theory, not random noise.
hint: Compute what a pure value-maximizer should do with any nonzero offer.

q: Offered a coin flip — win $21 on heads, lose $20 on tails — most people decline, and typically demand potential winnings near $40 before accepting. Kahneman and Tversky (1979) explained this pattern with which principle?
options: Losses loom larger than equivalent gains, so a bet must promise roughly double the loss to feel worthwhile
People are generally unable to compute expected values for small everyday sums
The endowment effect: people overvalue objects they have physically possessed for a long time
The status quo bias: refusing any gamble whatsoever is the easiest way of leaving one's situation unchanged
explain: Loss aversion, central to Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, holds that losses are felt roughly twice as intensely as equivalent gains. A near-fair gamble therefore feels bad overall, and the potential win must approach double the potential loss before the bet turns attractive.
hint: Weigh how the possible loss feels against the slightly larger possible gain.

q: Knetsch (1989) gave one group a mug, another a chocolate bar of similar value, and a third group nothing, then let everyone choose between the two goods. What did the gifted groups do, and what does it show?
options: They traded eagerly for the other item, showing that novelty outweighs ownership
They chose in the same proportions as the no-gift group, showing preferences are stable regardless of ownership
Most swapped for the unfamiliar item, suggesting people crave whichever option they do not yet possess
They overwhelmingly kept whatever they had been handed — mere ownership had inflated the item's value
explain: Both gifted groups strongly preferred keeping their own item — mug holders kept mugs, chocolate holders kept chocolate — while the no-gift group split roughly evenly. Ownership alone inflated each item's subjective value: the endowment effect, a close cousin of loss aversion.
hint: The no-gift group's even split is the baseline; compare the others against it.

q: In Kahneman and Tversky's outbreak scenario, 600 lives are at stake. Framed as gains, most people pick the sure option ('200 saved') over a gamble; framed as losses, most pick the gamble over '400 will die' — though the pairs are numerically identical. What does this reveal?
options: People are fundamentally risk-seeking when outcomes are described as gains and risk-averse whenever they are described as losses
Risk attitudes flip with framing: sure things attract when outcomes are cast as gains, gambles attract when the same outcomes are cast as losses
People cannot do probability arithmetic under emotional stress
The two versions differ in expected value, so the differing choices are rational
explain: Gain frames make the sure thing attractive (risk aversion); loss frames make the gamble attractive (risk seeking). Since the underlying numbers never change, the reversal violates expected utility theory's core assumption that preferences are independent of description.
hint: Track which frame makes people grab the sure thing and which makes them gamble.

q: After bilateral vmPFC damage, patients in Bechara et al.'s (2000) card-gambling study kept choosing decks with big immediate payoffs and larger long-run losses — while stating they knew the strategy was bad. How does the somatic marker hypothesis explain this?
options: vmPFC damage erases explicit memories of the previous losing hands
vmPFC damage abolishes the capacity to reason about long-term outcomes, so patients can no longer understand which strategy is optimal
Without the vmPFC, the gut emotional signals that normally tag risky options never arise, so knowledge fails to steer choice
vmPFC damage heightens anxiety so much that patients become too fearful to abandon familiar decks
explain: Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis holds that the vmPFC attaches bodily emotional signals — a flutter of anxiety, a warning gut feeling — to options under consideration. Lesions sever that channel, so intact abstract knowledge never receives the visceral tag needed to guide the actual choice.
hint: The patients' knowledge was intact; ask what signal failed to accompany it.

q: Countries where organ donation is the default (opt-out) show far higher enrollment than opt-in countries, and Pichert and Katsikopoulos (2008) found the same for green energy plans. Which bias do default-based nudges harness?
options: Loss aversion
The conjunction fallacy
Belief bias
Status quo bias
explain: Defaults exploit the status quo bias: people tend to leave arrangements exactly as they find them, so whichever option requires no action wins enrollment. Thaler and Sunstein's nudge program builds policy from precisely this kind of predictable inertia.
hint: The winning option is always the one requiring no action at all.
